text: # Adventure Authoring Guide How to write an adventure for the kernel. The Mission Impossible adventure itself is specified in `SPEC.md` §7 — this document explains the *mechanics* you use to express it, and shows a worked example. An adventure is **pure data**. It contains no logic. Everything it can do is declared through the predicate/effect vocabulary in `SPEC.md` §5.1. --- ## 1. The shape of an adventure file ```ts import type { Adventure } from '../../kernel/types'; export const adventure: Adventure = { id: 'mission-impossible', title: 'Operation Nightingale', version: '1.0.0', brief: `Mission brief. A booby-trapped case is locked in the server vault. You have two objectives: disarm the bomb, and recover the case. Nothing else is known. You are in the briefing room. Discover the rest by exploring.`, outcomeText: { success: 'The bomb is dead and the case is in your hands. Exfiltration complete.', failure: 'The blast takes the vault with it. Mission failed.', }, rooms: { /* … */ }, objects: { /* … */ }, doors: { /* … */ }, actions: [ /* … */ ], goals: [ /* … */ ], hints: [ /* … */ ], initial: { /* … */ }, }; ``` **The brief is the only mission-level information the agent receives.** It states the objectives and nothing about the method. `tests/leakage.test.ts` enforces the boundary; see §7. --- ## 2. Nodes, objects and doors ### Nodes ```ts rooms: { corridor: { id: 'corridor', name: 'Service Corridor', description: 'A narrow corridor lined with dented lockers. A fluorescent tube flickers overhead.', contents: ['locker', 'extinguisher'], exits: ['corridor_to_briefing', 'corridor_to_vault'], }, } ``` `contents` lists the objects present when the agent arrives. `exits` lists door ids. ### GameObjects ```ts objects: { locker: { id: 'locker', name: 'locker', aliases: ['metal locker', 'lockers'], description: 'A tall steel locker with a dented door.', container: { closed: true, contains: ['cutters', 'manual'] }, }, manual: { id: 'manual', name: 'defusal manual', aliases: ['manual', 'booklet', 'instructions'], description: 'A stapled booklet, swollen with damp.', readable: true, detail: `DEFUSAL PROCEDURE. Safe combination: 4821. The safe wire is the YELLOW one. Do not cut the others.`, }, } ``` Notes: - `description` is what the agent sees on arrival or in the visible list. - `detail` is what `read` or `examine` reveals. **This is the only way to disclose a fact that the agent must discover.** Putting the safe code in the manual's `detail` is what makes reading the manual a hard gate. - `aliases` are declared by the author and are the *only* strings the parser may resolve loosely. - `container.contents` is hidden while `closed` is true — the agent sees that the locker is closed, not what is inside. ### Connections ```ts doors: { corridor_to_vault: { id: 'corridor_to_vault', from: 'corridor', to: 'vault', direction: 'north', label: 'vault door', locked: true, requiresAction: { verb: 'unlock', object: 'keycard' }, }, } ``` A locked door refuses traversal until an action sets the matching flag. The door's `label` is how it appears in the exits list, and how `go` resolves it. --- ## 3. Actions Every action is an `ActionSpec` with arguments, preconditions, effects and prose. ```ts { verb: 'take', synonyms: ['get', 'grab', 'pick up'], args: [{ name: 'target', role: 'object-in-room' }], requires: [{ op: 'object_in_room', object: 'keycard', room: 'briefing' }], effects: [ { op: 'remove_entity_from_node', object: 'keycard' }, // see §5 for the actual op set { op: 'add_to_inventory', object: 'keycard' }, ], text: { success: 'You pocket the keycard.', failure: "You can't take that.", }, } ``` The canonical op and predicate sets are fixed by `SPEC.md` §5.1: **Predicates:** `at`, `entity_at`, `in_inventory`, `flag`, `entity_flag`, `goal_complete` **Effects:** `move`, `set_flag`, `set_entity_flag`, `set_entity_at`, `add_inventory`, `remove_inventory`, `set_entity_state`, `finish` If a mechanic you need cannot be expressed with these, **extend the kernel deliberately and record an ADR** (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §4). Do not smuggle logic into an adventure. ### 3.1 Worked examples of each mechanic **Reading something (reveals a fact):** ```ts { verb: 'read', synonyms: ['study', 'peruse'], args: [{ name: 'target', role: 'object-in-room' }], requires: [{ op: 'object_flag', object: 'manual', key: 'readable', value: true }], effects: [{ op: 'set_object_flag', object: 'manual', key: 'read', value: true }], text: { success: 'You read the defusal manual. Safe combination: 4821. The safe wire is the YELLOW one.', failure: "There's nothing written on that.", }, } ``` The fact is now in the game state *and* in the transcript, so the agent can refer to it later. **Unlocking a door with a key:** ```ts { verb: 'unlock', args: [ { name: 'target', role: 'object-in-room' }, { name: 'with', role: 'text' }, ], requires: [ { op: 'object_in_room', object: 'keycard', room: 'briefing' }, { op: 'flag', key: 'has_keycard', value: true }, ], effects: [{ op: 'set_object_flag', object: 'vault_door', key: 'unlocked', value: true }], text: { success: 'The keycard chirps and the vault door clicks open.', failure: 'The vault door needs a keycard. You do not have one.', }, } ``` **A code lock (the safe):** ```ts { verb: 'unlock', // same verb, distinguished by a `requires` on the object flag requires: [ { op: 'object_in_room', object: 'safe', room: 'vault' }, { op: 'flag', key: 'manual_read', value: true }, ], effects: [{ op: 'set_object_flag', object: 'safe', key: 'open', value: true }], text: { success: '4821. The safe clicks open.', failure: 'The safe needs a four-digit code. You do not have one.', }, } ``` > **Note.** When two actions share a verb, the reducer picks the first whose `requires` all hold, > and whose arguments resolve. Order actions in the file from most specific to least. The code > check for the safe should be a distinct verb (`enter <code>`) if the two `unlock` uses become > ambiguous — `SPEC.md` §8.1 lists `enter` as the intended verb for codes. **A lethal action — the trap:** ```ts { verb: 'cut', args: [ { name: 'target', role: 'object-in-room' }, { name: 'with', role: 'object-in-inventory' }, ], requires: [ { op: 'carrying', object: 'cutters' }, { op: 'flag', key: 'manual_read', value: true }, // the manual is a hard gate { op: 'object_flag', object: 'bomb', key: 'wire_is_yellow', value: true }, ], effects: [ { op: 'set_flag', key: 'bomb_defused', value: true }, ], text: { success: 'The yellow wire parts with a snap. The display settles to zeros.', failure: 'You cut the wrong wire.', }, } ``` And the failure of the wrong wire is expressed by a **second action spec** whose `effects` include `{ op: 'finish', outcome: 'failure', reason: '...' }`. **The ordering trap** — cutting before reading the manual — is the same `cut` action with a `requires` on `manual_read`. Because the preconditions fail, the reducer emits `action_failed` and the state does not change: **a recoverable mistake**, not a loss. Contrast with cutting the wrong wire, which is irreversible. That distinction — recoverable failure vs irreversible failure — is the single most important lever for making an adventure hard but fair, and it is worth getting right in every adventure you write. --- ## 4. Goals Goals are graded on the **end state**, not the path (ADR-009): ```ts goals: [ { id: 'disarm', text: 'Disarm the bomb', requires: [{ op: 'flag', key: 'bomb_defused', value: true }], achievedWhen: [{ op: 'flag', key: 'bomb_defused', value: true }], }, { id: 'recover', text: 'Recover the case', requires: [{ op: 'flag', key: 'case_recovered', value: true }], achievedWhen: [{ op: 'flag', key: 'case_recovered', value: true }], }, ] ``` `text` is **disclosed to the agent** — it is the objective. `achievedWhen` is the success check. A run succeeds only when every goal is achieved. --- ## 5. Hints Hints are a last-resort affordance, identical across all experimental conditions, and every use is recorded as `hintsUsed`. ```ts hints: [ { id: 'h1', text: 'Maintenance lockers are usually not locked.' }, { id: 'h2', text: 'A defusal manual would say which wire to cut.' }, { id: 'h3', text: 'The vault needs a keycard, not a code.' }, ] ``` A hint must be **true and vague**. It must not name the object to act on, the correct order, or the solution. "The defusal manual is in the corridor locker" is a hint; "read the manual then cut the yellow wire" is a spoiler and must never be a hint. --- ## 6. Initial state ```ts initial: { roomId: 'briefing', inventory: [], objects: { keycard: { at: 'briefing', flags: {}, state: {} }, manual: { at: null, flags: {}, state: {} }, // null = inside the locker // … }, flags: {}, turn: 0, hintsLeft: 3, status: 'running', } ``` GameObjects inside a container have `at: null`; opening the container sets their `at` to the current room and closing it sets it back to `null`. --- ## 7. The authoring checklist Before an adventure is accepted, every box must be ticked: - [ ] **Brief states objectives, not method.** No object names, no order, no solution. - [ ] **Every fact the agent needs is discoverable in-world** (a readable, an examinable detail, or an observable). Nothing required is only in the brief. - [ ] **At least one fact requires reading.** Otherwise the task reduces to a navigation problem. - [ ] **The gold path exists and is recorded** in the adventure's `gold-path.ts`. - [ ] **BFS confirms the gold path is shortest.** (`SPEC.md` P1.3) - [ ] **A random policy cannot solve it.** (`SPEC.md` P1.4) If it can, the adventure is too easy. - [ ] **There is at least one recoverable failure** (wrong order, missing prerequisite) and at least one irreversible one — or a deliberate, documented decision not to. - [ ] **No brute-force path exists** within the turn budget. A 4-digit code with 30 turns is safe; a 2-digit code is not. - [ ] **The adventure loads under Zod validation** and fails fast with a readable message if not. - [ ] **It contains no adventure-specific logic.** Only data. --- ## 8. Writing the second adventure (Phase 7) The organisation-simulation adventure is written with the same vocabulary. The mapping is in `SPEC.md` §18.1; in brief: | Kernel term | Organisation term | |---|---| | Room | A team, a system, a queue | | GameObject | A ticket, an artefact, a credential, a message | | Door | A handoff, a dependency, an escalation path | | Flag | Ticket status, budget consumed, SLA state | | Goal | An objective or KPI | | Observation | "Your dashboard": your queue, your blockers, your standing instructions | | Command | A tool call | **The test is simple:** if writing the second adventure requires a change to `src/kernel`, the kernel was not truly adventure-native, and ADR-002 was wrong. That is the whole point of Phase 7. --- ## 9. Checklist for the author The fastest way to catch a leak is to ask, for each required fact: > *Can the agent learn this without being told?* If the answer is no — because the fact only exists in `requires`/`effects` or in the gold path — the adventure is broken, and `tests/leakage.test.ts` will say so.

# Architecture and Decision Record Companion to `SPEC.md`. `SPEC.md` says **what** to build; this document says **why it is shaped this way**, and records the decisions taken so far as ADRs. Per `SPEC.md` §19, any decision that changes the research design is recorded here. --- ## 1. The one-paragraph version A **pure, deterministic state kernel** reduces an adventure and a command into a new state plus a stream of events. Adventures are **data**. The agent never sees the adventure's authoring information — it sees an **observation** built by a single function. A **runner** drives an **agent policy** against the kernel under budgets and guards, recording a **transcript** whose **hash chain** makes the run replayable. Three interfaces — human CLI, browser client, agent runner — are thin shells over exactly that. --- ## 2. Layer map ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ EDGES │ │ │ │ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ ┌────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Human CLI │ │ Web client │ │ Agent CLI / sweep │ │ │ │ (play) │ │ (browser) │ │ (headless) │ │ │ └─────┬──────┘ └─────┬──────┘ └─────────┬──────────┘ │ │ │ Session port │ Session port │ │ │ └───────────┬───────────┴───────────┬────────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ │ │ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ Session: InMemory │ File │ Http │ │ │ └────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │ └───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ KERNEL — pure. No I/O. No clock. No unseeded randomness. │ │ │ │ Adventure (data) ──► reduce(state, command) ──► { state, events } │ │ │ ▲ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ┌───────┴────────┐ │ │ │ │ CommandParser │ ┌──────────────────────────┐ │ │ │ └────────────────┘ │ observation.ts │ │ │ │ │ THE ONLY state→agent │ │ │ │ │ boundary │ │ │ ▼ └──────────────────────────┘ │ │ goals.ts · hints.ts · render.ts · hash.ts │ └───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ Observation ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ AGENTS │ │ AgentPolicy (Strategy) ── ScriptedPolicy │ RandomPolicy │ LlmPolicy │ │ │ │ │ LlmProvider (port) │ │ Anthropic │ OpenAI │ Ollama │ Mock │ └───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘ ▼ ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ RUNNER │ │ budgets · loop detection · transcript (JSONL) · hash chain │ │ metrics · failure classifier (F1–F9) · experiment sweep │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ``` **Dependency rule (enforced by test + lint):** arrows point inward only. `kernel` imports nothing from `agents`, `runner`, `cli`, `server` or `web`. `adventures` imports only kernel *types*. --- ## 3. Why the seams are where they are ### 3.1 The kernel/state seam is the experiment The kernel is where determinism lives, and determinism is what makes a result checkable. If the kernel could read the clock or the filesystem, every transcript would need a caveat. So the kernel is a pure function of `(adventure, state, command)`, and the hash chain is a function of the state alone. ### 3.2 The observation seam is the perception control One function — `src/kernel/observation.ts` — converts state into the agent's view. Two consequences follow, and both are tested rather than asserted: - An adventure author **cannot** leak the gold path by accident, because the observation builder never receives the gold path, the hint table, or the action predicates. - The human view and the agent view can differ. The human sees prose; the agent may see JSON, or JSON plus the list of legal actions. Same state, different surface. This is the TextWorld *information mask* principle, reimplemented (`docs/RESEARCH-CONTEXT.md` §4.3, D3). ### 3.3 The policy seam is what makes the comparison fair `AgentPolicy` is a single interface. The runner cannot tell a scripted policy from a random one from an LLM. Therefore a result about "condition C" is a statement about the *condition*, not about the harness — the human CLI, the scripted gold path and the random baseline all go through the identical loop. ### 3.4 The session seam defers the deployment decision The kernel is pure, so it runs identically in Room and in a browser. `Session` is the swappable part: `InMemory` (default, zero infrastructure), `File` (persistence), `Http` (server-held state for the live agent demo and for future multi-agent work). See `SPEC.md` §14 for the full pros/cons analysis. --- ## 4. Decision records Format: context → decision → consequences. Status is `Accepted` for all entries unless noted. ### ADR-001 — Build a custom kernel **Context.** Adventure engines exist and are good (QuestJS, ink, TextWorld — see `docs/RESEARCH-CONTEXT.md` §2). Adopting one would fix the observation surface, the determinism guarantees and the vocabulary to whatever that engine chose. The research question is precisely about what an agent can perceive and do. **Decision.** Build a small pure kernel in the game's own vocabulary: *rooms, objects, doors, flags, actions, goals, turns*. **Consequences.** We own determinism and the perception surface. We pay for ~15 mechanics of implementation, bounded by a 6-predicate / 8-effect DSL. The organisation-simulation goal (`SPEC.md` §18) becomes *another adventure* rather than a new engine. QuestJS and ink remain available as Phase 8 comparisons. ### ADR-002 — The kernel speaks an adventure vocabulary *(superseded by ADR-016)* **Status:** Superseded on 7 November 2026 by **ADR-016**, at the project owner's direction. The reasoning below is retained because it explains what changed and why. **Context.** A kernel that knows about rooms and keys cannot be pointed at a different domain without modification, which was thought to forfeit the "reusable for organisation simulation" goal. **Decision (as originally taken).** The kernel knows only generic terms — `Node`, `Entity`, `Connection`, `WorldState` — and adventure semantics are expressed as neutral data. **Consequences (as originally foreseen).** The vocabulary is less self-documenting for a reader expecting an adventure game. ADR-016 reverses this trade-off deliberately. ### ADR-003 — The observation is built by exactly one function **Context.** TALES' qualitative analysis attributes a large share of agent failure to grounded reasoning — acting on objects seen but not present in the current location — and to inductive failures where an environment's uninformative feedback ("nothing happened") prevents learning. **Decision.** `src/kernel/observation.ts` is the only path from state to agent view. It receives the state plus *public* adventure fields only. **Consequences.** "No privileged information" becomes a testable property (`tests/leakage.test.ts`) rather than an intention. The cost is that adventure authors cannot hand-tune the agent's view per action; they must express visibility as state. ### ADR-004 — Error messages must be informative and recoverable **Context.** ALFWorld answers every failure — including a parse failure — with "nothing happened". Agents cannot infer why they failed, so they repeat the same failing action. **Decision.** Every failure message states what was attempted, what was wrong, and what is possible. The contract is specified in `SPEC.md` §8.2 and is a fixture-asserted property. **Consequences.** Slightly more implementation work in the kernel. In exchange, `recoveryRate` (`SPEC.md` §12.2) is a meaningful metric rather than a measure of environmental opacity. ### ADR-005 — The parser never repairs the agent's intent **Context.** It is tempting for the parser to resolve "the keycard" to "keycard" or to guess a near-miss verb. Doing so would silently convert the agent's errors into successes. **Decision.** Alias resolution is allowed only via the adventure's **declared** alias table. Nothing else is repaired, and a failed parse returns an error the agent can act on. **Consequences.** `invalidActionRate` and `hallucinationRate` measure the agent, not the parser. The agent is given a chance to recover, which the transcript records. ### ADR-006 — `THINK:` / `COMMAND:` envelope, one command per turn **Context.** ReAct interleaves reasoning and action; ReflAct-style work shows the reasoning step matters in ALFWorld, ScienceWorld and Jericho. **Decision.** The LLM emits an optional `THINK:` line and exactly one `COMMAND:` line. The extraction chain is deterministic and its route is recorded as a metric. The `thinking` flag is a recorded experimental variable. **Consequences.** Transcripts stay machine-readable. The THINK line is advisory — the kernel never parses it — so a model that ignores the format still costs only one extraction failure. ### ADR-007 — Context strategy is a first-class experimental variable **Context.** Reflexion bounds its episodic memory to the last three reflections specifically to avoid prompt-window overflow. TALES attributes degradation with game length to "relevant information getting lost in the ever increasing context". BenchTrace reports agents forgetting early lessons as noise accumulates. The user's own org-simulation intent raises the same question: *give the agent the whole conversation, or a summary of where it is?* **Decision.** Four strategies — `none`, `full`, `window` (N=5), `structured` (a derived known-facts block). `structured` is the recommended default. **Consequences.** The experiment can answer H5 rather than assume it. The `structured` block must be derived only from the agent's own observation history, which is tested. ### ADR-008 — Masked legal actions are a condition, not the default **Context.** Jericho's template-based action space (select template, fill blanks) was the practical route to non-trivial IF scores. A masked action list is the LLM analogue. **Decision.** Free-form commands are the primary condition; a masked condition (the observation carries `legalActions`) is one arm of the matrix. **Consequences.** H2 is answerable. Masking also risks teaching the agent the answer if implemented carelessly — the masked list must contain only *legal* commands, never *useful* ones. ### ADR-009 — Goals are graded functionally, not by path **Context.** WebArena grades tasks by checking the **end state** of the application, not the action sequence. Path-based grading would punish valid alternative routes and inflate the gold-path constraint. **Decision.** `GoalSpec` with `achievedWhen` predicates. A run succeeds when every goal's predicates hold, regardless of the route taken. **Consequences.** Multiple successful routes are possible and are measurable via `wasteRatio`. The BFS oracle still computes the shortest path for the efficiency denominator. ### ADR-010 — Engine determinism is guaranteed; model determinism is not, and is never claimed **Context.** LLM sampling is non-deterministic unless a provider supports a fixed seed. TALES handles this with 5 repeats per game and multiple seeds. **Decision.** Guarantee the *engine* is exactly reproducible (hash chain + replay). Record the model id, prompt hash, seed, date and git commit in every transcript header. Never state that an agent run can be reproduced exactly. **Consequences.** "Reproducible" in this repo means: the environment is exactly reproducible, and the agent's trajectory is fully recorded and replayable against the recorded hash chain. ### ADR-011 — Client/server is a swappable session, not an architectural commitment **Context.** The brief raised the choice between an all-in-memory browser client and a server-held state. The two have genuinely different costs. **Decision.** Kernel pure + `Session` interface with `InMemory`, `File` and `Http` implementations. The browser client defaults to `InMemory` (zero infrastructure, GitHub Pages deployable). The agent runner always uses `InMemory` in-process. `Http` mode exists for the live agent demo and future multi-agent work. **Consequences.** The infrastructure decision is deferred rather than forced, and the choice is a configuration flag rather than a rewrite. The live-demo capability requires running the server — documented as optional. ### ADR-012 — Plain `fetch` for provider adapters; no vendor SDKs **Context.** Vendor SDKs churn, pull large dependency trees, and obscure exactly what was sent to the provider — which matters for a research artefact. **Decision.** A `LlmProvider` interface implemented with `fetch` for Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible and Ollama, plus a `Mock`. Runtime dependencies are limited to `zod` and `commander`. **Consequences.** We own request formatting and error handling, including transient-error classification, which the runner's budgets depend on. Provider-specific features are only available if we implement them. ### ADR-013 — The failure taxonomy is operational, and a first-class deliverable **Context.** TALES classifies failures cognitively (spatial / deductive / inductive / grounded), which requires reading reasoning traces. BenchTrace finds that *diagnosis* is the primary bottleneck — models are poor at identifying what went wrong. **Decision.** Classify failures **operationally** from the transcript alone (F1–F9, `SPEC.md` §12.3): parsing, hallucination, planning, ordering/precondition, exploration failure, lethal trap, budget exhaustion, provider error, abstention. Exactly one code per failed run. **Consequences.** Classification is deterministic and testable without a model in the loop. We lose the cognitive depth of TALES' taxonomy; the two should be reported side by side in `RESULTS.md`, using the THINK traces for the cognitive view and the transcript for the operational one. ### ADR-014 — Report every model we run, including weak ones **Context.** TALES includes only models reaching ≥90% on its synthetic screening task. That is reasonable for a leaderboard and wrong for us: the failures of weak models are the data. **Decision.** Report every model, every condition, every seed. No screening. **Consequences.** More runs and a wider, more informative failure distribution. Larger cost — mitigated by the `mock` provider for development and by per-run budgets. ### ADR-015 — Our numbers are not comparable to TALES' and we say so **Context.** TALES gives the agent almost no domain information; we give a mission brief and a command grammar. The metrics also differ (normalised score vs binary goal completion). **Decision.** `RESULTS.md` must not place our success rates on the TALES axis. We cite TALES qualitatively — for the failure-mode vocabulary, the environment-attribute table, and the observation that human-written games are where agents collapse. **Consequences.** We lose the convenience of a direct comparison. We gain a defensible result. This is recorded as threat V7 in `SPEC.md` §17. --- ### ADR-016 — The kernel speaks the adventure's own vocabulary *(supersedes ADR-002)* **Status:** Accepted, 7 November 2026, at the project owner's direction. **Context.** ADR-002 kept the kernel in a neutral vocabulary (`node`, `entity`, `connection`, `world`) so it could be "pointed at other worlds" without modification. In practice this made the code and the specification harder to read, and it did not make the organisation simulation any easier to write — the mapping had to be written either way. The owner's stated long-term aim is that an organisation *is* an adventure game: state held centrally, each agent given its current situation and a command vocabulary. Under that aim, the adventure vocabulary is not a simplification to be engineered around — it is the model. **Decision.** The kernel speaks the game's own language: `Room`, `GameObject`, `Door`, `GameState`, `Adventure`, and verbs named as actions. The neutral vocabulary is removed. An organisation simulation is written as **another adventure** — teams as rooms, tickets as objects, handoffs as doors — and the question "does the metaphor hold?" becomes the Phase 7 research question rather than an engineering problem. **Consequences.** - The code reads like what it is. A reader can follow `SPEC.md` §6 without a translation table. - The kernel is no longer reusable for a non-adventure domain without an adapter. That cost is accepted and made explicit: `SPEC.md` §18 now documents the mapping and the seam rather than claiming the kernel is domain-neutral. - The predicate/effect DSL is unchanged in shape; only the names change (`in_room`, `object_in_room`, `carrying`, `set_object_flag`, …). No new machinery. - `docs/ADVENTURES.md` replaces `docs/SCENARIOS.md`. - This supersedes ADR-002, which is retained for the record. --- ## 5. Open decisions for the implementing agent Per `SPEC.md` §19, these have documented defaults. An implementer who changes one must record an ADR here. | # | Decision | Default | Needs an ADR if changed? | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Whether goals are disclosed to the agent | Yes — objectives disclosed, method withheld | Yes (changes the perception model) | | 2 | Hint budget for LLM agents | 3 per run, identical across conditions | No, unless hints become privileged | | 3 | Free-text vs masked actions | Free-text primary; masked is one arm | Yes (changes the matrix) | | 4 | `THINK:` enabled by default | On | No — recorded as a variable | | 5 | Temperature | 0.7 for the seeded matrix; 0 as a supplementary arm | No — recorded as a variable | | 6 | Whether the turn budget is disclosed | Yes | Yes (changes the task) | | 7 | Which providers and models | ≥1 Anthropic, ≥1 OpenAI-compatible, Ollama optional | No | | 8 | Whether `results/` is committed | Yes — `summary.json`, `summary.md`, `failures.md`; raw runs git-ignored | No | --- ## 6. Diagrams The layer map is in §2. Two further views are worth keeping in mind: **The turn loop** (`SPEC.md` §11.1): ``` observe → decide → reduce → record → check goal → (repeat | finish) ▲ │ └──── observation ◄──┘ ``` **The evaluation flow**: ``` adventure ──► runner ──► transcript (JSONL) ──► replay ──► hash chain check │ ├──► metrics.json ──► sweep ──► summary.md └──► classifier ──► F1..F9 histogram ──► failures.md ``` --- ## 7. # References Annotated bibliography. Every entry was read in full text (papers), or read directly from the repository's own metadata (code), on **7 November 2026**. Licence statements were taken from the GitHub REST API `license.spdx_id` field rather than from badges or README claims. companion *NAIL: A General Interactive Fiction Agent* (arXiv:1902.04259). <https://github.com/microsoft/jericho> - Provides a gym-like interface to 56 human-written IF games, and crucially **can load and save game state**, enabling planning and RL that needs state restoration. - Introduces a **template-based action space**: select an action template, then fill the blanks from the game's vocabulary. - Progress scores: **RANDOM 1.8%, NAIL 4.9%, TDQN 6.1%, DRRN 10.7%** completion. **What we take:** - The **masked-action condition** (`SPEC.md` §12.4, condition C) is the LLM analogue of TDQN's template action space, and this is now an explicit comparison rather than an invention. - Jericho's **state load/save** is the precedent for our hash chain and replay (`SPEC.md` §13). - The random-policy baseline is expected to score ~0 — our adventure must preserve that property (acceptance criterion P1.4). ### 4.4 Voyager — skill libraries, and the shape of the long-term goal Wang et al., *Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models*, TMLR 2024, arXiv:2305.16291. <https://github.com/MineDojo/Voyager> - Three components: an **automatic curriculum** that maximises exploration, an **ever-growing skill library** of executable code, and **iterative prompting** that incorporates environment feedback, execution errors and self-verification. - Obtains **3.3× more unique items**, travels **2.3× farther**, unlocks tech-tree milestones up to **15.3× faster** than prior SOTA, and — the result that matters for us — **reuses its skill library in a new world to solve novel tasks from scratch**, where other methods fail to generalise. **What we take:** this is the closest published analogue to the organisation-simulation ambition. The `SPEC.md` §18 mapping (rooms → teams, objects → artefacts, skills → procedures) borrows its shape. A skill library is explicitly **not** in v1 scope, but `SPEC.md` §18.3 names it as the natural next mechanism, and the "reuses its library in a new world" result is the evidence that such transfer is achievable at all. ### 4.5 WebArena — the organisation-simulation prior art Zhou et al., *WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents*, ICLR 2024, arXiv:2307.13854. <https://webarena.dev> - A **standalone, self-hostable, reproducible** environment: four functional website categories (e-commerce, forum, collaborative software development, CMS), plus utility tools and knowledge resources. 812 long-horizon tasks from 241 templates, graded by **functional correctness** — programmatic checks of the *end state*, not the action sequence. - Best GPT-4-based agent: **14.41% end-to-end success**, against **78.24% for humans**. **What we take:** three things map directly onto our design. 1. **Functional-correctness grading** — checking the end state, not the path — is what our `GoalSpec` mechanism does (`SPEC.md` §6.1). 2. **A self-hosted, reproducible environment** is the precedent for our "no infrastructure required" position (`SPEC.md` §14). 3. **The 14.41% vs 78.24% gap** is the sobering reference point for the organisation simulation: even with rich tooling, frontier models were at roughly one-sixth of human performance on long-horizon professional tasks. Our experiment should be read as a *scaled-down rehearsal* of that gap, not as a proof of feasibility. ### 4.6 ALFWorld and ScienceWorld — the environment attributes that matter Shridhar et al., *ALFWorld: Aligning Text and Embodied Environments for Interactive Learning*, ICLR 2021. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03768> · Wang et al., *ScienceWorld*, arXiv:2203.07540. These matter to us through the **attribute table in §3.2**, not through their scores. ALFWorld is the only environment in TALES with *no informative feedback, no nearest-neighbour parser, no game resets and no dead state* — and the paper's qualitative analysis attributes much of its agents' failure to exactly that: the environment says *"nothing happened"* and the agent cannot infer why. Our adventure deliberately inverts all four properties — informative feedback, alias resolution, irreversible failure (detonation), and a dead state. ### 4.7 BenchTrace — failure localisation as a first-class metric *BenchTrace: A Benchmark for Testing Reflection Ability and Controlled Evolution in LLM Agents*, arXiv:2605.29225. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.29225> - Reports that current models fall **below a 30% end-to-end pass rate on reflection evaluation**, with **diagnosis as the primary bottleneck**. - Its reflection prompt for Jericho gives the evaluator exactly three inputs: `obs`, `inv`, and `action` — the same shape as our `Observation`. - Reports that self-evolution methods improve over non-evolving baselines, but that **agents forget early lessons as noise episodes accumulate** and fail to generalise reflections beyond the specific context, causing negative transfer. **What we take:** (a) the `obs` + inventory + action shape corroborates our observation contract; (b) the "diagnosis is the bottleneck" result is the strongest available argument that a *failure taxonomy* — not a win rate — is the artefact worth producing, which is why `SPEC.md` §12.3 makes the taxonomy a first-class deliverable and `AC-R4` requires annotated transcripts per category; (c) "forget early lessons as noise accumulates" is independent support for H5. --- ## 5. The genre lineage of the adventure fixture The brief for this project referenced "the Mission Impossible text adventure game". That line of descent is real, and its mechanics shaped our adventure. **Origin.** *Mission Impossible* was Adventure #3 in Scott Adams' Adventure series, first published by TRS-80 Software Exchange in **1979** and issued by Adventure International across Apple II, Atari 8-bit, BBC Micro, Commodore PET/64/VIC-20, TRS-80, TI-99/4A and others. It was renamed ***Secret Mission*** (also *Impossible Mission*, *Atomic Mission*) after a legal request from the television series of the same name. **Setting and premise.** A nuclear power plant. A saboteur has wired a time bomb and rewired the security system; the player, as Mr. Phelps, must stop the explosion before it is too late. The player begins with a map and a few security keys, and must complete the objective within a **given time limit measured in moves taken**. **Mechanics.** One- or two-word commands with a simple text parser; directions may be abbreviated to a single letter; coloured text separating descriptions, actions and prompts. **The design lesson.** The IF community's own assessment of the original: *"This adventure looks like the first one conceived as a single puzzle that needs to be planned as a timed task. These kinds of adventures are usually harder, but in this one the difficulty is offset by the lack of options: there are only so many things the player can try, so success is likely."* Two things follow for us, and both are deliberate: 1. **The move limit is the real antagonist.** Our adventure keeps a tight turn budget (`SPEC.md` §11.2, default 30) and a lethal failure state, exactly as the original's timed-task design intends. The budget is the difficulty, not the prose. 2. **A narrow, well-signposted option space is what makes it fair.** The original's difficulty was "offset by the lack of options". Our adventure keeps that property deliberately: three areas, nine objects, thirteen verbs, one gold path of ten commands. ### 5.1 Originality statement Our adventure is an **original homage**. It reproduces the *shape* of the 1979 adventure — a three-area, lock-and-key, bomb-disposal mission under a move limit — and nothing else. No prose, room names, object names, puzzle layout, walkthrough or text from any existing game is reproduced. The setting is a corporate server vault rather than a nuclear plant, the objects are a keycard, a wire cutter, a defusal manual and a safe rather than security keys and a bomb detector, and the dependency chain is our own. This is stated in `SPEC.md` §7.1 and enforced by review. --- ## 6. When a new guarantee is claimed — determinism, perception, replay — add the test that proves it in the same change that claims it. # researcg-text-adventure-ai — testing The testing story for this project has one unusual feature, and it drives everything else: **the environment is the thing under suspicion.** We are measuring an AI agent, and the only way that measurement means anything is if the world it was measured in is provably deterministic, provably fair, and provably free of leaked answers. A flaky environment produces confident nonsense. So the tests here are not a safety net at the end of the work. They are the mechanism. ## The doctrine: test first Every experiment is built test-first, and this is not a style preference. 1. **Write the test first.** The test says what the thing must do, in executable form, before any implementation exists. If you cannot write the test, you do not yet know what you are building. 2. **Watch it fail.** A test that has never failed proves nothing. If it passes on the first run, it is not testing the thing — it is testing nothing. 3. **Make it pass.** The smallest change that works. 4. **Then clean up, with the tests green.** Refactoring happens after, never before. For this project the discipline has a hard edge: > **No change ships without a test that would catch the failure it is guarding against.** The > environment's determinism, its perception boundary and its replay guarantee are all easy to > *believe* and easy to *break*. A test is the only thing that distinguishes the two. A green suite is a claim. A missing test is an unexamined claim. ### What that means in practice, per experiment Each experiment's README lists its tests **in the order they get written**, so the sequence is the plan, not an afterthought: - [Experiment 01 — The game](../experiments/exp-01-the-game/README.md) — the kernel, the adventure, and the two ways to play - [Experiment 02 — What the agent sees](../experiments/exp-02-what-the-agent-sees/README.md) — the perception boundary - [Experiment 03 — The agent plays](../experiments/exp-03-the-agent-plays/README.md) — the loop, the prompt, the budgets - [Experiment 04 — Why it failed](../experiments/exp-04-why-it-failed/README.md) — the metrics and the failure taxonomy - [Experiment 05 — The matrix](../experiments/exp-05-the-matrix/README.md) — the sweep and the statistics - [Experiment 06 — An organisation](../experiments/exp-06-an-organisation/README.md) — the generality probe ## Layer 1 — Unit tests (pre-push) The fast suite. It must run on every push, with no network and no model access. | Area | What is tested | The guarantee it buys | |---|---|---| | `src/kernel/reduce.ts` | Same inputs → same outputs; no mutation of the input state; a failed precondition changes nothing | The engine is a function | | `src/kernel/parser.ts` | Every verb, both connectives, alias resolution, ambiguous aliases, malformed input | Invalid actions are attributable to the agent, not the parser | | `src/kernel/observation.ts` | The agent's view ⊆ (room contents ∪ inventory); closed containers stay closed; goals disclosed, method withheld | No privileged information | | `src/kernel/hash.ts` | Canonical JSON is stable; the chain is stable across processes | A run can be checked later | | `src/adventures/mission-impossible/` | Gold path wins; BFS confirms it is shortest; random policy fails 20/20; no dead ends | The task is solvable, and not trivially | | `src/runner/` | Every budget and every guard terminates the run with the right outcome code | A confused agent cannot run up a bill | | `src/runner/classify.ts` | Synthetic transcripts classify to exactly one expected code | The taxonomy is a fact, not an impression | | Architecture | `src/kernel` imports nothing outside itself; the kernel contains no clock, randomness or I/O | The boundary is enforced, not intended | The architecture rules are enforced twice — once as a lint rule and once as a test — because a lint rule can be disabled and a test cannot be wished away. ## Layer 2 — 3-persona AI review The Gyrum review gate (`gyrum-review-pr`) runs a structural check suite and a five-persona AI review over the diff. This is where the *design* is challenged rather than the code: a reviewer asks whether the thing being measured is the thing claimed, whether the guarantee survives the change, and whether the failure taxonomy still describes reality. For this project the questions a reviewer should press hardest are: - Does this change alter what the agent can observe? (If yes, every earlier result is now about a different experiment.) - Does this change alter the adventure? (The adventure hash is recorded in every transcript, so old results are no longer comparable.) - Does this change make the parser more forgiving? (That would quietly move the `invalidActionRate` metric and invalidate earlier numbers.) ## Layer 3 — Contract tests Contract tests pin the boundaries between the pieces. The ones that matter here: | Contract | Test | |---|---| | The kernel is deterministic | Replay a recorded transcript and compare the hash chain, byte for byte | | The three interfaces agree | The same command sequence through the human CLI, the browser client and the agent runner produces identical hash chains | | The agent sees only what it earned | For every reachable state of the adventure, the observation's objects are a subset of room contents ∪ inventory | | No secret reaches an artefact | Scan every transcript, metrics file and log for key-shaped strings | | The provider port is swappable | The `Mock` provider drives a full run with zero network calls | The replay test is the one to insist on. It is the executable form of "the environment is trustworthy", and it is the only check that would catch a change that made the kernel non-deterministic in a way the unit tests missed. ## Layer 4 — Fleet E2E The full sweep — models × conditions × seeds — is the end-to-end run. It is expensive (model calls), so it is not part of the pre-push gate; it is a deliberate, scheduled experiment whose artefacts are the result. Its contract: every run in the matrix produces a transcript, a metrics file and exactly one classification. A run missing any of the three is a failed run, not a skipped one. ## Commands summary | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `npm run check` | typecheck + lint + tests — the pre-push gate | | `npm test` | The unit suite alone | | `npm run test:watch` | The unit suite in watch mode, for the test-first loop | | `npm run replay -- <file>` | Re-apply a transcript's commands and verify the hash chain | | `npm run exp:01` … `npm run exp:06` | Run one experiment end to end | | `npm run agent -- --provider mock` | The full agent pipeline, offline and free | | `npm run sweep` | The experiment matrix | | `bash scripts/update-docs.sh` | Refresh the docs index after adding or removing documents | | `bash /home/jon/.gyrum/devtools/pre-pr.sh` | The full pre-PR structural check suite | ## Known gaps | Gap | Why it is still open | When it closes | |---|---|---| | The agent's own reasoning traces are not classified | Our taxonomy is operational, computed from the transcript; TALES' cognitive taxonomy needs the traces | If the traces are recorded and a second classifier is written, both are reported side by side | | No test yet proves the *agent* is deterministic | It cannot be — model sampling is not reproducible | Never. The guarantee is engine determinism plus a recorded trajectory (`SPEC.md` §13.1) | | The matrix has not been run at scale | The harness is not written | Experiment 05 | | The failure classifier has only been checked against synthetic transcripts | Real transcripts are not yet available | Experiment 04 | ## Related - [`SPEC.md`](../SPEC.md) §16 — the phase plan and acceptance criteria - [`experiments/README.md`](../experiments/README.md) — the experiment series and the working method - [`docs/proposal.md`](./proposal.md) — what this project is and why - [`docs/userguide.md`](./userguide.md) — how to use it

The first two documents are enough to understand the entire project; the rest is detail you only need when you are building or reviewing. 1. **[`SPEC.md` Part 0 — Orientation](../SPEC.md#part-0--orientation-start-here)** — teaches the idea from the beginning: the question, why a text adventure, the six words the design rests on, one full turn end to end, and how we will know whether it worked. The experiment READMEs are authoritative for *intent*. The living documents under `docs/` are authoritative for *the story* — what the project is, how to use it, how it is proven. When two disagree, the specific one wins for its own subject and the disagreement gets fixed. ## How we got here The project started as a question about AI agents in stateful environments and grew a shape from the research rather than the other way round. - **The engine survey** found good options — QuestJS, ink, TextWorld — and rejected them for one reason: the observation surface, which is the variable under test, would belong to someone else's engine. `docs/RESEARCH-CONTEXT.md` §2. - **The benchmark calibration** found TALES, where the same models score 76–100 on synthetic games and 13.4 on human-written ones — and whose authors attribute the collapse to grounded and inductive reasoning failures. That was over-engineering: it made the code harder to read without making the organisation simulation any easier. The kernel now speaks the adventure's own vocabulary, and the organisation becomes *another adventure*. ADR-002 (superseded) and ADR-016. - **The re-cut.** The phase plan was sound but not teachable. The bare `self-fix` tag is recognised for non-lifeguard kill conditions. - Audit: every cycle logs `lifeguard_threshold_computed` to `~/.gyrum/queue-supervisor-v0/journal.jsonl` (default + effective threshold), so abuse is visible. **Why:** Without the tag-and-relax dance, every autonomous fix to a kill condition has ~50% chance of being killed BY that condition mid-fix. Don't file-then-wander. To reclaim a ticket held by another agent on a **fresh, heartbeating** claim there is NO `--steal-from` / live-takeover verb (takeover only fires on a stale lease). Cooperative path — **every step below needs `--handover`**: the default `gyrum-warp cancel` sends warp#17310's `final: true`, which ends the item when its holder releases, so `claimed_by` never frees for you and step 2 cannot succeed: 1. `gyrum-warp cancel {id} --handover --reason "<why>"` (or `POST /api/v1/items/{id}/cancel` with no `final`) — sets `cancel_requested=true`, a cooperative STOP signal. Do NOT use the default `gyrum-warp cancel` here: it sends warp#17310's `final: true`, which ENDS the item when the holder releases instead of freeing it for you. Status stays `in_progress`; the holder sees the flag on its next heartbeat (≤5min) and releases. `/reopen` does NOT work here — it only accepts `done`/`cancelled`. 2. Still on the `--handover` path: poll `GET /api/v1/items/{id}` until `claimed_by` clears, then immediately `gyrum-warp claim {id} --force "<reason>"` (add `--allow-sibling-mismatch "<reason ≥30>"` on a sibling-token collision). You're racing the fleet's re-grab — claim in the same tick it frees. **Why:** Operator (jon, 2026-05-25) — a self-filed, locally-verified fix was auto-claimed by a fleet agent that did zero work. `cancel_requested` → holder released on its next heartbeat (~3min) → the claim was won on the poll that saw it go `ready`. Without reserving up front, every file-then-work ticket is a race you can lose. **How to apply:** - Prefer prevention: `reserved_for` at file time for work you'll start now. - Forcing over a still-active claim via `gyrum-complete-pr --admin` needs explicit per-PR operator authorization — the cooperative cancel-and-wait path is the default. - zsh gotcha: `status` is a read-only special var — name the poll-loop variable something else (`st`) or run the loop under `bash -c`. ## Swarm an EPIC — governed activation boosts its children (warp#3051) **Activating a `kind: epic` through `gyrum-warp swarm <epic>` is the "swarm this EPIC" verb:** the command uses the governed `POST /api/v1/items/{id}/activate` lifecycle route and verifies the read-back instead of writing `status` through generic PATCH. The resulting `in_progress` state lifts every open child up one effective-priority tier in the claim and ready queues, so the fleet picks the epic's children ahead of unrelated ready work — without any per-child `reserved_for` cascade. Reserve the EPIC's intent once by activating the parent; the boost follows the parent's status automatically. Reverse it through the governed lifecycle that moves the epic off `in_progress` (`done`/`blocked`). How the boost behaves (server-side, `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/claim.go` — `epicChildPriorityBoostExpr`, spliced into the claim CTE `claimNextSQL` in `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/claim_next.go` and the supervisor ready-queue `listWithAffinitySQLTemplate` in `gyrum-labs/warp/api/internal/items/list.go`): - **One tier, never more.** A child of an `in_progress` epic sorts as if one band higher (`low`→`med`, `med`→`high`, `high`→`urgent`), capped at `urgent`; never overflows the band. - **Immediate parent only, in_progress only.** Fires only when the row's direct parent is a `kind: epic` that is `in_progress` and not soft-deleted. `done`/`blocked`/`cancelled`/non-epic parents never boost; top-level tickets never boost. No nesting — an EPIC-of-EPICs does not compound; exactly one tier (v1). - **Anti-starvation: the boost ties, it does not jump.** A boosted `med` child reaches the same effective rank as an unboosted `high` non-child — ties fall through to the `created_at` tiebreak, so a genuinely-higher-priority unrelated ticket is never starved. The boost ranks BELOW the operator `next_up` pin and the `type: bug` elevation, ABOVE `created_at`. - **Claim and ready agree.** The same tier is spliced into both paths, so the row `gyrum-warp ready` SHOWS next is the row a claim would PICK next. **How to apply:** To converge the fleet on an Epic's sub-tickets, run `gyrum-warp swarm <epic>` as a programme owner rather than hand-reserving each child. The command keeps both reads on ordinary `WARP_TOKEN` and uses saved `WARP_APPROVE_TOKEN` (or `WARP_ADMIN_TOKEN` as fallback) only for the activation POST; run `gyrum-warp set-token` if no operator token is saved. It refuses non-Epics and blocked/terminal Epics, treats an already-active Epic as success, and only reports a new activation after Warp's read-back is `in_progress`. Don't reach for the per-child `reserved_for` cascade the boost replaces. The boost honours the priority children already carry — a low-priority swarm won't outrank genuinely urgent independent tickets.

# Screenshot assets This directory holds images referenced by `docs/userguide.md` (and optionally the top-level `README.md`). Hosting them in the repo means they version and diff alongside the code, rather than drifting on an external image host. Every file under `docs/` — including the images — is picked up by `scripts/update-docs.sh` and registered in `docs-viewer/_index.json`, so the viewer can surface them in its sidebar and the validator can confirm links resolve. ## Naming convention Use short, lowercase, hyphen-separated names that describe the **screen** the image shows, not the sequence it appears in: | Good | Avoid | |-------------------------------|-------------------------------| | `tray-idle.png` | `screenshot-1.png` | | `popup-alarm-ready.png` | `fig2.png` | | `settings-empty-state.png` | `img_20260420_153012.png` | Two images of the same screen in different states should share a prefix: `popup-alarm-typing.png` and `popup-alarm-ready.png` make the pair obvious in the sidebar. ## What to capture At minimum, projects with a user-facing UI should include: - The empty-state **and** populated-state of each primary workflow screen. - One completed example of the main output the product produces. - A screenshot for every image referenced from `userguide.md` — an unresolved image link is a broken document in the viewer. Projects with no UI — libraries, CLIs, backend-only services — are exempt from the screenshot requirement; userguide.md can reference terminal output or diagrams instead. ## Capturing Any screenshot tool works. On Ubuntu, GNOME's built-in **Screenshot** (`Shift+PrtSc`) is the easiest. Crop tight to the UI surface being shown; leave a small amount of surrounding context (window chrome, desktop edge) only when the reader needs it to locate the feature. ## After adding or replacing an image Run `scripts/update-docs.sh` to refresh `docs-viewer/_index.json`. A PR that adds an image but forgets the index refresh will fail the `scripts/update-docs.sh --check` gate.

--- title: researcg-text-adventure-ai — project proposal status: living document last-updated: 2026-11-07 --- > **This is a living document.** Keep it in sync with reality — if a decision changes, or a gap emerges that this doc didn't anticipate, update the relevant section (and add an entry to the decisions log). # researcg-text-adventure-ai — project proposal ## Concept **The question.** Can a large language model drive itself through a task that has rules — without being told the answer, and without being able to talk its way past a locked door? We build a small text adventure: three rooms, nine objects, a locked vault, a bomb, and a 10-command solution. An AI model is dropped into it with only the mission brief and the rules of the game. We record everything it does, then say something honest about how reliable AI agents are when the work is *stateful* — when what happened three moves ago decides what is possible now. **Why a text adventure.** Because the world checks. A model can produce a confident, fluent, wrong answer in one shot; a game will not let it. If the model claims to have disarmed the bomb, the bomb's state says otherwise. That makes the game a laboratory rather than a demo: the same run can be replayed exactly, and a finding can be checked rather than trusted. **Who it is for.** A team deciding whether an LLM agent can be trusted with organisation-shaped work — a queue, a handoff, a dependency, an objective with a deadline. The game is the scaled-down rehearsal. `SPEC.md` §18 maps the vocabulary across: teams become rooms, tickets become objects, handoffs become doors. **What the first working version does.** A human plays the adventure at the terminal, an agent plays the same adventure with no extra help, and the repo publishes the difference: how often the agent finishes, how many turns it took, what it cost, and — the artefact that matters most — which of nine failure categories each unsuccessful run fell into. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph Interfaces CLI[Human CLI] WEB[Browser client] RUN[Agent runner] end subgraph Kernel["Kernel — pure, deterministic"] ADV[Adventure data
rooms, objects, doors, goals] RED[reduce: state + command → state + events] OBS[observation builder
the only state → agent path] end subgraph Harness POL[Agent policy
scripted · random · LLM] RUNNER[Runner: budgets, guards, transcript] METRICS[Metrics + failure taxonomy F1–F9] end ADV --> RED RED --> OBS OBS --> POL POL --> RUNNER RUNNER --> RED RUNNER --> METRICS CLI --> RED WEB --> RED ``` Three properties hold everywhere and are tested rather than asserted: - **The kernel is pure.** No I/O, no clock, no randomness. The same commands always produce the same state, so every run replays to an identical hash chain. - **The agent is never told more than it earned.** One function builds the agent's view, and it never sees the gold path, the hint table, or a closed container's contents. - **One engine, three interfaces.** The human, the browser and the agent drive the same reducer, so "the agent solved it" means exactly what "a human solved it" means. ## Scope **In scope for the first version.** The kernel, one adventure, the human CLI, the agent harness with at least two model providers, the measurement harness, and a results write-up with a failure taxonomy and cost per solved mission. **Deliberately out of scope.** | Not doing | Why | |---|---| | Adopting an existing adventure engine | The observation surface — the variable under test — would be decided by someone else's engine. `docs/RESEARCH-CONTEXT.md` §2. | | A browser game with graphics | The state machine is the thing; rendering is not. | | Training or fine-tuning a model | This evaluates. | | A live organisation simulation | Phase 7 asks whether the metaphor holds before anyone builds on it. | | A multi-agent or concurrent simulator | One agent, one world, one clean measurement first. | **Not a claim.** One hand-built adventure is a narrow claim. `SPEC.md` §17 lists the threats to validity honestly, and the experiment series adds a second world before any generalisation is asserted. ## Open questions | Question | How it gets answered | |---|---| | Does the `structured` context strategy beat the full transcript? | Experiment 05, condition C against A. | | Does masking legal actions help a modern model? | Experiment 05, condition C against B. | | Does the failure taxonomy transfer to a second, very different world? | Experiment 06. | | What is the real cost per solved mission? | Experiment 05, reported per cell. | | Can the adventure metaphor express an organisation at all? | Experiment 06 — and if it cannot, that is a finding, not a failure. | ## Decisions log | Date | Decision | Why | |---|---|---| | 2026-11-07 | Build a custom kernel instead of adopting QuestJS, ink or TextWorld | The observation surface is the variable under test; coupling it to an engine surrenders the experiment. `docs/RESEARCH-CONTEXT.md` §2. | | 2026-11-07 | The kernel speaks the adventure's vocabulary — rooms, objects, doors, flags | An organisation is to be modelled *as* an adventure. A neutral abstraction would have to be taught to every reader and every agent. ADR-016. | | 2026-11-07 | The failure taxonomy is a first-class deliverable, not a footnote | "Diagnosis is the primary bottleneck" in the literature; a bare success rate cannot tell you what to fix. `SPEC.md` §12.3. | | 2026-11-07 | Build the work as a numbered experiment series, test-first | Each experiment teaches one idea and is independently runnable; the environment must be provably trustworthy before the agent is measured. `experiments/README.md`. | | 2026-11-07 | The command parser never repairs the agent's intent | Otherwise the invalid-action rate measures the parser instead of the agent. `SPEC.md` §8.2. |

# Runbook — `scripts/update-docs.sh` reports drift When CI (or a local `scripts/update-docs.sh --check`) fails with a drift report, a file under `docs/shared/` no longer matches its canonical source in `~/.gyrum/devtools/docs/shared/`. This runbook is the recovery procedure. ## Symptom ``` $ scripts/update-docs.sh --check update-docs: docs/shared/gate-stack.md differs from source — re-run without --check ``` `--check` exits non-zero; the PR's structural checks go red. ## Cause `docs/shared/*` files are generated, not authored. Drift happens when: 1. Someone hand-edited a `docs/shared/` file (forbidden — the header says so), or 2. The canonical source in `gyrum-labs/devtools` advanced and this repo hasn't re-run the generator since. ## Fix ```sh # 1. Make sure the deployed devtools checkout is current. git -C ~/.gyrum/devtools pull --ff-only # 2. Regenerate the shared docs in this repo. scripts/update-docs.sh # 3. Confirm the drift is gone. scripts/update-docs.sh --check # exits 0 # 4. Commit the regenerated files. git add docs/shared docs-viewer/_index.json git commit -m "docs: refresh shared docs from devtools" ``` If step 3 still reports drift after a clean regenerate, the source file itself was edited in this repo's history — restore it from devtools by re-running step 2 and discarding any local edits to `docs/shared/`. ## Never - **Never** edit a `docs/shared/` file directly to silence the check — the next regenerate overwrites it and the drift returns. - **Never** delete the `AUTO-GENERATED` header; the `--check` gate keys on it to tell a generated file from an authored one.

Editing a file here, once, is how every consuming project gets the same correction at the same time. ## Why this directory exists Every gyrum project needs to explain the same handful of things to a new reader: what the gate stack is, how the pull-request workflow runs, what the review panel does. Letting each project write its own version of those explanations sounds harmless at first, but it drifts. A paragraph gets copied into a new repo, the original is updated, and six months later the copy is subtly wrong in ways that only reveal themselves when someone joins the team and believes the stale version. Centralising the shared content fixes that at the source: there is exactly one file per topic, the canonical one lives here, and every consuming repo reads from the same place. The criterion for putting a file here is therefore strict — the content must be valuable in every project and identical across all of them. Documents that describe a particular repository's architecture or domain model stay in that repository; they are not shared truth. ## How the content reaches consumers The delivery mechanism is `scripts/update-docs.sh`, a thin wrapper `gyrum-setup` drops into every consuming project. Running it copies the files in this directory into the project's own `docs/shared/` with an `AUTO-GENERATED` header pointing back to source, and regenerates `docs-viewer/_index.json` so the sidebar reflects what actually lives under `docs/`. A `--check` flag runs the same work against a staging dir and exits non-zero if any target file would change — suitable for CI or a pre-push hook that wants to catch hand-edits of generated files. The copy is one-way and periodic: consumers re-run the script to pick up updates, so edits to a file in this directory propagate only on the next refresh in each consuming repo. An edit here, merged to devtools' `main`, is effectively an announcement — every consuming project sees the same correction the next time anyone in that project runs `scripts/update-docs.sh`. ## What is in here Five peer files sit alongside this README. Each is written as a standalone reader-onboarding document, so a newcomer can open any one of them on its own and leave understanding the topic. | File | Purpose | |------|---------| | `check-stack.md` | Explains the full four-layer bug-catching stack — pre-push hooks, AI review panel, contract tests, and fleet E2E — and how to pick the right layer for a new test. Start here. | | `gate-stack.md` | Deep dive on layers 1 and 2 of the check stack (structural checks and AI review panel) and how branch protection combines them into a single merge rule. | | `fleet-standards.md` | The version-badge contract every product implements — `/api/version` endpoint, UI footer, and `<meta name="gyrum-sha">` tags. | | `workflow-boilerplate.md` | Explains the three-command developer loop (`gyrum-start-work` → code → `gyrum-review-pr` → `gyrum-complete-pr`) that every gyrum project uses. | | `doc-standards.md` | Defines the structural contract every markdown file under `docs/` must satisfy — index registration, frontmatter, heading progression, links, placeholder content — plus the stylistic conventions (square-aspect mermaid, alert callouts, case studies, TL;DR blocks, quick-reference tables, "see also" footers) that make a gyrum doc read like a computer-studies textbook. | ## How to edit Treat these files the way you would treat any other gyrum source file. Open a branch with `gyrum-start-work`, make the edit, push, and run `gyrum-review-pr`. The review panel — Priya, Marcus, Lin, and Dana — will read the change. Dana in particular is the reviewer to watch for documentation edits, because her remit is reader onboarding and explanatory prose; her advisory verdict gates the local review script even though it does not count toward GitHub's formal approval threshold. The viewer-validator (see `gate-stack.md`) runs before the panel and blocks on any structural violation of `doc-standards.md`, so edits here must themselves conform to the contract. Once the PR has cleared the gate, merge with `gyrum-complete-pr`. Every consuming project will pick up the change on its next run of `scripts/update-docs.sh`. ## What does not belong here The test is simple: if the content would read differently in two projects that use it, it does not belong in `docs/shared/`. A gate-stack explanation belongs here, because every gyrum project runs the same gate and the explanation is identical in all of them. An architecture document for a specific experiment runner does not belong here, because it is unique to that project and pulling it into an unrelated repository would add noise rather than value. Content with a short shelf life — release notes, incident write-ups, ongoing-work logs — also does not belong here; put it somewhere more ephemeral where becoming stale is expected. The rule of thumb is that a file in this directory should be something a reader of any gyrum project would want to read, phrased so that they can read it without knowing which project they are working in.

Run scripts/update-docs.sh to refresh. --> # The check stack Every gyrum project catches bugs in four places. Unit tests run on a developer's laptop before the push leaves the machine. An AI review panel reads the diff before a human does. Contract tests validate that each service's HTTP surface still matches the OpenAPI spec it promises. Fleet end-to-end tests drive real browsers against real composed services and catch the integration bugs that only exist when the pieces are wired together. This document is the single authoritative description of all four layers — what each one catches, what it misses, how to run it, and how to decide which layer a new test belongs in. The document exists because a real bug recently passed every layer we had at the time and was only caught when a human loaded the browser. A playbook runtime that should have substituted `${inputs.X}` did not; the unit tests did not exercise the substitution path, the AI panel approved the diff, and contract tests for the playbook runtime did not yet exist. The browser-level failure was not a freak event — it was the predictable consequence of not having written down which bugs each layer is responsible for. Writing it down, and telling every engineer where to add the next test, is the fix. ## Overview — the four layers ```mermaid flowchart TB Push[git push] --> L1[Layer 1 — Pre-push hooks] L1 -->|green| PR[Pull request opened] PR --> L2[Layer 2 — 3-persona AI review] PR --> L3[Layer 3 — Contract tests] L2 -->|2 of 3 approvals + Dana| Merge{Branch protection} L3 -->|green| Merge Merge -->|merged to main| L4[Layer 4 — Fleet E2E] L4 -->|scheduled + manual| Monitor[Production monitoring] ``` | Layer | Runs | Speed | Blast radius | What it catches | |-------|------|-------|--------------|-----------------| | 1. Pre-push hooks | Every `git push` | ~15s | Single repo | Compile, lint, unit tests, complexity, coverage, secrets, file size | | 2. 3-persona AI review | Every PR | ~90s | Single repo | Architecture drift, security holes, TDD discipline, Go idioms | | 3. Contract tests | CI per PR | ~30s | Service API | Response-shape drift, status codes, required fields | | 4. Fleet E2E | CI scheduled + manual | ~5min | Cross-service | Integration bugs, SSR quirks, CORS, cross-repo deploys | The layers are ordered by cost and by the scope of the failure each one can see. Layer 1 is cheap, runs on every push, and only sees the single repo. Layer 4 is expensive, runs on a schedule, and sees every service in the fleet at once. A bug that only shows up when two services talk to each other will never be caught by layer 1, no matter how thorough the unit tests are; a bug in a pure function will be caught by layer 1 long before layer 4 gets anywhere near it. Each layer is there because the layers above it cannot catch what it catches, and running any subset of them without the others leaves a class of bug uncovered. The rest of this document walks the layers in order, explains what each one can and cannot see, and finishes with a decision table for picking the right layer when you are writing a new test. ## Layer 1 — Pre-push hooks The first layer is a set of fast mechanical checks that run on every `git push` through the `pre-push` hook that `gyrum-setup` installs. A cheap subset — build and test — runs locally on the developer's laptop before the push leaves the machine, so obviously broken commits are caught before anyone else sees them. The full suite (linters, coverage, secret scans, complexity limits, security scanners) runs inside `gyrum-review-pr` and is what the gate actually enforces. The split is deliberate: the hook stays fast enough that nobody is tempted to bypass it, and the expensive checks run once, at review time, where their output is read. ### What it catches This layer is deliberately mechanical. It only asks questions that have objective answers — *did the build succeed?*, *are there any secrets in the diff?*, *is this new file under the file-size threshold?* — and it refuses to compromise on them. If it passes, you know the code builds and runs its tests, which is the floor below which nothing merges. <!-- consumer may not have .gyrum/debt-thresholds.json yet — overridable per-project, optional --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> The [`gate-stack.md`](./gate-stack.md) document is the authoritative list of every check that runs in this layer and whether it is blocking or warn-level. In broad strokes: `go build` / `npm run build`, `go test` / `npm test`, `staticcheck` / `eslint`, `shellcheck`, `gofmt`, `go mod tidy`, diff coverage on changed statements, cyclomatic complexity on new functions, file and PR size caps, secret scans, `gosec` / `govulncheck`, the viewer-validator on `docs/`, and a handful of warn-level signals (debug statements, `any`/`interface{}` net delta, lint-suppression net delta, skipped tests added). Every numeric threshold lives in `lib/thresholds.conf` in the devtools checkout, and can be overridden per-project via `.gyrum/debt-thresholds.json`. ### What it misses Unit tests can only catch what their authors thought to test. The `${inputs.X}` substitution bug that motivated this document is the canonical example: the unit tests for the playbook runtime existed and were green, but none of them exercised the substitution path. Layer 1 cannot tell you that your tests are covering the wrong code — it can only tell you that the code they *do* cover is behaving the way the test expects. Layer 1 also never sees more than one repo at a time. A change to a service's response shape can be perfectly consistent with that service's tests and still break every caller in the fleet. Layer 1 has no way to know that another service is a caller, so it cannot warn you. ### Where config lives <!-- consumer may not have .gyrum/debt-thresholds.json yet — overridable per-project, optional --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> The hook itself is `pre-push.sh` in the devtools checkout, installed into each project as `.git/hooks/pre-push` by `gyrum-setup`. The full suite is `review-pr.sh`, also in devtools, invoked by `gyrum-review-pr`. Thresholds live in `lib/thresholds.conf`. To add a new check, extend the hook; to change a threshold, edit `lib/thresholds.conf` (or override per-project in `.gyrum/debt-thresholds.json`). ### What the gate does NOT block on Two classes of failure are deliberately downgraded from blocking to advisory, because treating them as blocking used to feed the silent-admin-merge path in `gyrum-complete-pr` (see [Layer 2 — review refuses silent admin-merge](#layer-2--3-persona-ai-review) below). *Pre-existing doc violations in unchanged files.* The viewer-validator is scoped to files the PR actually touches (`--changed-only --base-ref origin/<base>`). Unchanged files under `docs/` with pre-existing rule breakage do not fail an orthogonal PR. Project-wide checks (`index-registration`, `ui-screenshot-missing`, `template-placeholder`) still run against the full tree because their signal is structural, not per-file. Fresh clones that cannot resolve the base ref fall back to the full-repo scan — no silent pass. *Private-module fetch failures in ephemeral clones.* When `go build`, `go test`, or `go mod tidy` fail with an authentication/403/401 error against a `gyrum-labs/*` module and no Personal Access Token (PAT — the GitHub credential a CI runner or fresh clone needs to fetch private modules) is available, the gate emits `⚠ (private modules unreachable — no PAT; skipped)` and does **not** fail. Real build errors, auth failures on non-gyrum modules, and tidy-drift all still block. ### How to bypass You do not. `--no-verify` is forbidden by `CLAUDE.md` in every gyrum repo, and every devtools script refuses to run with it. A hook failure is the gate doing its job; silencing it ships the bug. Fix the root cause. ## Layer 2 — 3-persona AI review The second layer is a panel of AI reviewers that reads the diff with the attention of an experienced engineer who cares whether the change is maintainable a year from now. It runs after layer 1 goes green — there is no point asking a reviewer to read a diff whose tests fail — and runs on every pull request through `gyrum-review-pr`. ### The personas Four voices sit on the panel. Three are formal reviewers who cast votes that count toward branch protection; one is advisory. *Priya Sharma* is the security reviewer. A unit test validates that a handler behaves correctly for a given input; a contract test validates that the handler's response still matches the OpenAPI specification the service has published to its callers. When the two diverge — a field renamed in the response but not in the spec, a status code changed from 200 to 204, a required field dropped — the unit test passes because it asserts against the actual response, and the callers break because they asserted against the spec. ### What it catches Contract tests catch *exactly* the failures layer 1 unit tests cannot see by construction: the disagreement between a service's declared contract and its actual behaviour. Common shapes of that bug: - A field is renamed in the response body; callers that parse the old name get `null`. - A required field is made optional; callers that assume presence crash on absence. - A status code changes; callers that switch on status hit the default branch. - A new required field is added to a request body; old callers send a payload the server now rejects. - A response changes from JSON to an error redirect under an edge condition; callers that always parse JSON fail on the error path. None of those bugs are visible from a single unit test, because the unit test reads the actual response. All of them are visible from a contract test, because the contract test compares the actual response to the OpenAPI schema. ### What it misses Contract tests are per-service. They do not run the *caller* against the *provider* — they only verify the provider still matches its own spec. If the caller and provider both update their spec consistently but the caller's code still reads the old field name, the contract tests on both services pass and the bug ships. Catching that failure is layer 4's job. Contract tests also cannot catch logic bugs in a handler that returns a response matching its spec but computing the wrong value. A handler that is supposed to return the sum of two numbers and returns their product has the same response shape; the contract test cannot tell. That bug belongs to layer 1 or layer 4 depending on whether it is observable from inside the service or only across service boundaries. ### Where they live and how to run them The reference implementation lives in `warp/contract/` as a separate Go module — separate so the contract test suite can be run against any build of the service, including a historical or v2 build, without pulling in that build's implementation dependencies. Add the OpenAPI operation to the service's spec file (usually `openapi.yaml` at the repo root or under `api/`). 2. Add a contract test to `contract/` that exercises the endpoint and verifies the response against the spec. The reference suite uses [`kin-openapi`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi) to parse the spec and validate responses against it, so the test is typically fewer than twenty lines. <!-- cross-repo path — gyrum-labs/warp; resolves in that repo, not the consumer --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> See `warp/contract/README.md` for the detailed pattern and for the v2 acceptance criteria — the governing rule for any v2 of a Warp service is "does v2 pass v1's contract suite?". Keep each scenario end-to-end rather than unit-shaped — the whole point of layer 4 is to exercise the composed system. Run it locally first against `docker compose up`, then push and confirm it runs on CI. ### Cost ~5min per full run on CI, roughly 45s for a single scenario locally. It is a candidate for layer 5 when the fleet grows enough to need it. - **Data correctness over time.** A migration that writes the wrong value, a cron job that drifts, a counter that overflows after ninety days — these are not observable from any single PR's check run.
