Beyond the structural contract, a *good* gyrum doc reaches for square-aspect mermaid diagrams, alert callouts, case studies pinned to real PRs, TL;DR blocks, quick-reference tables, and a curated "See also" footer — the vocabulary that turns a shared snippet into something a reader actually wants to read. ## Overview Every gyrum project grows a `docs/` tree, and every gyrum project ships a `docs-viewer/` next to it so that reading the tree is one command away. The two only keep their promises to the reader if the files inside `docs/` follow a shared shape — the sidebar lists every document, the headings form a clean outline, the mermaid blocks render, the links resolve. This document is the contract that defines that shape. It governs the *structural* properties that the viewer and the automated validator care about, and it also collects the stylistic conventions — callouts, diagram shape, case studies, reference tables — that make a gyrum doc read like a computer-studies textbook rather than a wall of unbroken prose. A reader finishing this file should be able to look at any markdown file under `docs/` and answer both "is this a conformant gyrum doc?" and "is it a *good* one?" with confidence. The contract is written against `docs-viewer/README.md` (which describes how the viewer actually renders files) and `docs/shared/README.md` (which describes how shared snippets are pulled into each project). Read both if you want the full picture of why each rule exists. The high-level shape of a conformant, well-written gyrum doc looks like this: ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Structure["Structural — validator-enforced"] direction TB idx[Index entry] fm[Frontmatter] hd[H1 + progression] lk[Relative links] end subgraph Style["Stylistic — preference"] direction TB tldr[TL;DR block] cal[Callouts] dia[Square mermaid] cs[Case studies] sa[See also footer] end Structure --> Doc[Conformant gyrum doc] Style --> Doc Doc --> Reader[Happy reader] classDef success fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745 classDef neutral fill:#e2e3e5,stroke:#6c757d class idx,fm,hd,lk,tldr,cal,dia,cs,sa neutral class Doc,Reader success ``` Structural rules on the left are machine-checked and block merges. Stylistic guidance on the right is preference rather than gate — the difference between a doc that passes and a doc that a reader actually enjoys. ## Scope The rules below apply to every markdown file under `docs/` in a consuming project — both hand-authored documents and the auto-generated copies under `docs/shared/`. They do **not** apply to `CLAUDE.md` at the repository root, the top-level `README.md`, any prose embedded in source files (godoc comments, JSDoc, header banners), or release artefacts like `CHANGELOG.md`. Those have their own norms and conventions, and folding them into the same contract would conflate "a doc the viewer renders" with "any piece of writing in the repo". Everything under `docs/` is in scope; everything outside it is out. ## Index registration Every file under `docs/` must appear in `docs-viewer/_index.json`, because that file is the sole source of truth for what the viewer shows in its left sidebar. A file that is not registered is invisible to the viewer even when it sits two directories away, and an invisible document is effectively undocumented — it has no way to be discovered by a reader who came in through the viewer. The authoritative way to keep the index honest is to let `scripts/update-docs.sh` regenerate it: the script walks the project's `docs/` tree, filters by the allow-listed extensions, and writes out a nested tree sorted directories-before-files and case-insensitively by name. Hand-editing the index is permitted but discouraged, because the same scan runs again the next time anyone refreshes shared docs, and any manual ordering that disagrees with the scan will be overwritten. The structural validator treats drift between the on-disk tree and `_index.json` as a failure. If you add, rename, or remove a file under `docs/` without running `scripts/update-docs.sh`, the PR will not merge. The fix is a single command. ## Numeric-prefix naming for ordered documents When a folder under `docs/` contains files that have a natural reading order — a tutorial walked top to bottom, a pipeline described layer-by-layer, a vision → architecture → implementation narrative — the files must be named with a two-digit numeric prefix (`01-`, `02-`, …) or a letter prefix (`A-`, `B-`, …) so the sidebar's alphabetical-by-name sort matches the intended reading order. A folder whose files are *not* ordered — a glossary, a grab-bag of reference pages, a per-persona set of runbooks — is free to use plain names. The distinction is whether a reader is meant to traverse the folder in sequence or pick out the one page they need. The failure mode this rule prevents is a reader opening the sidebar, seeing `architecture.md`, `broker.md`, `iteration-2.md`, `library.md`, `pipeline-internals.md`, `pipeline.md`, `README.md`, `roadmap.md`, `tooling.md`, `vision.md` in alphabetical order, and starting at `architecture.md` when the author meant them to start at `vision.md`. Two digits because growing past ten files is common; zero-pad because `2-` sorts after `10-`. - `README.md` and `_index.md` stay at the root of the folder without a prefix. They are conventionally pinned to the top of the sidebar by most viewers and the numeric entries fall in sequence after. - If the ordering is primarily chronological (session logs, release notes), prefer a date prefix (`2026-04-24-session.md`) over a sequential number — dates sort naturally. - Renumber when the order changes rather than leaving gaps. A **living document** is one that tracks decisions, open questions, ongoing work, or anything else that can go stale as the project moves — proposals, design notes, architecture snapshots, findings logs. A **non-living reference document** is one whose content is static: a contract like this one, a shared snippet under `docs/shared/`, an operational runbook that documents an unchanging procedure. The viewer recognises the normal set of language tags that highlight.js ships with; there is no project-specific allow-list. Mermaid diagrams are a special case. A fenced block whose language tag is `mermaid` is handed to mermaid.js and rendered as an SVG diagram inline. Mermaid is the preferred notation for flows, state machines, sequence diagrams, and any other structural picture that would otherwise be drawn in a screenshot. A mermaid block is versionable text, diffs cleanly in review, and renders identically in every viewer instance; a pasted screenshot is none of those things. Reach for mermaid first, and only fall back to an image when the shape genuinely is not expressible as a mermaid diagram. ## Icons in docs Icons are welcome but earn their place. They're glyphs with meaning, not decoration. Every icon should be answering a question a reader might otherwise have to infer from prose. ### Where icons belong - **Callout labels** — paired with the callout type (📖 case study, 🧪 example, 🎯 try this, 🕳️ deep dive, ⚠️ pitfall, 🔖 glossary). These are the canonical set; don't invent new ones per doc. - **Mermaid diagram nodes** — when the node represents a real UI affordance (⚙ settings, ✏ edit, 🔒 locked) or a system role (🤖 agent, 👤 human, 📦 service). Use ascii-ish characters or unicode symbols, not emoji, when the diagram may render in terminals. - **Section markers for repeated structural elements** — e.g. "## 🧪 Worked example:" as an H2 consistently through a tutorial document. Consistency matters more than variety. - **Status / state indicators in tables** — ✓ done, ⏳ in progress, ✕ blocked, — n/a. Prefer these over words like "yes"/"no"/"pending" for dense reference tables. ### Where icons do NOT belong - **H1 titles** — keeps the sidebar list clean and greppable. - **Decorative flourishes in prose** — 🚀 to mean "fast", 💡 to mean "idea". The prose should carry the meaning. - **Every bullet point** — reads as noise. - **Replacing a word** — icons supplement, not substitute. "Deploy 🚀 the service" is worse than "Deploy the service." ### Icon vocabulary (canonical set) Use these consistently across docs so readers build intuition: | Icon | Meaning | |---|---| | 📖 | Case study (real past incident/PR) | | 🧪 | Worked example (code + output) | | 🎯 | Try this (actionable step) | | 🕳️ | Deep dive (optional tangent) | | ⚠️ | Pitfall (common mistake) | | 🔖 | Glossary (inline term definition) | | ✓ | Done / passed | | ⏳ | In progress / waiting | | ✕ | Blocked / failed | | — | Not applicable | | 🤖 | Agent / automation | | 👤 | Human / operator | | 📦 | Service / component | | 🔒 | Gated / requires approval | | 📍 | "You are here" in a flow | ### Accessibility Every icon paired with text — the icon is the visual affordance, the text is the semantic content. A screen reader user should understand the doc just as well without the icons. If an icon is alone (rare), include a `title` attribute or prose fallback. ### Terminal renderability Some icons don't render in terminal viewers (Unicode fallbacks vary). For docs that might be read via `less` or `cat`, stick to ASCII-compatible glyphs: ✓ ✕ — + -. The emoji callout set IS allowed in the viewer-rendered docs because gyrum-docs-viewer guarantees emoji support, but be conservative in any file likely to be grepped or piped to a terminal. ## UI screenshots <!-- consumer may not yet have docs/userguide.md — scaffolded by setup-project for UI-shipping repos --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> Projects that ship a user-facing UI must include screenshots of the primary screens in `docs/userguide.md` (and optionally the top-level `README.md`). At minimum: the empty-state and populated-state of each primary workflow screen, plus one completed example of the main output the product produces. Host the images under `docs/images/` in the repo so they version and diff alongside the code rather than living on an external host. Screenshots complement the mermaid-first rule for diagrams; they are the right choice for showing *what a screen actually looks like*, where mermaid is the right choice for *what a flow looks like*. Projects with no UI — libraries, CLIs, backend-only services — are exempt. ## PR functional and visual evidence Keep evidence inside the existing PR `## Verification` section. Production UI screen/rendering changes require a renderable image, mockup or functional preview. Backend API, data, state or authority changes require a small relevant flow, sequence or state diagram and an explanation of the changed boundaries. Root and nested module paths count alike. Mixed changes need both; UI-only needs no backend diagram and backend-only needs no screen preview. Documentation, tests, fixtures and unrelated scripts need neither visual shape; existing execution requirements for other work types still apply. Each UI record uses `visual-kind`, `artifact`, `route` or `function`, `scenario`, `source` and `caption`. Choose exactly one honest kind: **design mockup**, **local compiled preview** or **deployed screenshot**. Name the actual full source commit SHA and explain what the artifact shows. A design mockup must not claim runtime or deployment success. Local artifact paths must stay within the repository, exist and match `artifact-sha256`; their source must match the checked-out HEAD. A remote image or functional-preview record is **supplied-not-fetched**: the offline predicate never fetches its URL or verifies its contents, rendering or relevance. Formal reviewers judge relevance; a well-formed link alone is not verified visual content. The following shapes are templates, not evidence. Fill every field from actual artifacts; placeholders, example graphs and bare test-spec filenames cannot satisfy the requirement. Keep each record's fields together under its H3. ````markdown ### UI evidence visual-kind: local compiled preview artifact: ![screen](<existing local artifact path>) route: <route shown; use function instead when appropriate> scenario: <state or interaction shown> source: <full actual source commit SHA> caption: <what this shows> artifact-sha256: <actual local file SHA256> ```` For backend evidence, use `backend-diagram` with real Mermaid flowchart/graph, sequence or state relationships and a `boundary` explanation. An API diagram accompanies its existing curl execution evidence; a diagram alone is explanatory evidence and never runtime proof. Preserve any other required migration, CI or CLI execution evidence. ````markdown ### backend-diagram boundary: <which API, data, state or authority boundaries changed> ```mermaid <actual flow, sequence or state relationships> ``` ```` Generated recommendations remain visibly incomplete until filled. Seeding preserves author-written sections and is idempotent. This forward amendment leaves historical evidence meanings, advisory/enforce modes and audited exemptions unchanged; it grants no installation, protection or activation authority. ## Links <!-- the absolute-path token is cited as a non-compliant example; it intentionally does not resolve --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> Internal links between documents must be relative paths to files that are themselves registered in `_index.json`. A link like `[the gate stack](./gate-stack.md)` resolves correctly inside the viewer because the target is a sibling document that the index knows about; a link like `/docs/shared/gate-stack.md` or a bare `gate-stack.md` without the relative prefix does not, because the viewer serves from one directory above `docs-viewer/` and absolute-style paths escape that root. Linking to an unregistered file is equivalent to linking to nothing — the viewer may load the file if the path happens to resolve, but the reader has no way to navigate to it through the sidebar, which defeats the point. The validator treats both categories — non-relative internal links and links to unregistered files — as broken, and a broken link is a merge blocker. External links to the public internet are unrestricted. Use them freely where they point at authoritative upstream references. ## Placeholder content <!-- consumer may not yet have these scaffold paths — scripts/setup-project.sh, docs/proposal.md, docs/userguide.md are dropped by gyrum-setup, not assumed pre-existing --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> `scripts/setup-project.sh` drops template documents — `docs/proposal.md` and `docs/userguide.md` — into every new project so that the structural shape is present from day one. A template is a prompt to fill out, not a document to merge. A PR that lands a template-seeded doc whose content is still the template's own prose, with no project-specific content, is a failure: the doc claims to describe the project but in fact describes no project in particular, and letting it merge poisons the `docs/` tree with documents that look populated but are empty. The validator compares each template doc against the seed text and fails the PR when the match is too close. The fix is to write the document — the presence of the template is the starting point, not the finish line. ## Architectural decision records (ADRs) Architecturally-significant changes must be accompanied by an Architectural Decision Record in the repository where the change lands. An ADR is a short, immutable note that captures a single decision, the context that forced it, the alternatives that lost, and the consequences the team accepts by taking it. The purpose is historical: six months from now someone should be able to reconstruct *why* the system looks the way it does from nothing but the repo — no Slack archaeology, no tribal memory, no ad-hoc reconstruction from a half-remembered thread. ADRs are the shape that record takes across every gyrum project, so that the reasoning behind one project's design is legible to someone arriving from another. An ADR is required when the change is any of the following: a new component, service, or library that other code will depend on; a public API change that will outlive a single PR (signature, protocol, on-wire format); a security-relevant choice (authn/authz model, secret handling, redaction, trust boundary); an infrastructure change that constrains future deploys (new stack component, storage engine, runtime dependency); or a cross-cutting pattern that multiple services are expected to adopt (logging shape, error taxonomy, probe contract). A bug fix, a refactor, a dependency bump, or a piece of internal plumbing that could reasonably be reverted without stakeholder discussion does not need an ADR — the bar is "a future architect or security reviewer needs to understand why we chose this", not "we changed code". ADRs live at `docs/decisions/` in the repository where the change lands. File names use a zero-padded three-digit number followed by a short kebab-case slug: `007-redaction-phase-1-and-phase-1-5.md`. To number a new record, find the highest existing `NNN-` prefix in that directory and increment by one. Numbers are never reused — even a superseded record keeps its slot, because the slot is part of the historical trail the ADR set exists to preserve. Every ADR uses [Michael Nygard's template](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions) exactly. Four sections, in order: **Context** (the forces at play, why this needs a decision *now*), **Decision** (one crisp sentence in present tense, then the shape), **Consequences** (what becomes easier, what becomes harder, what we have signed up to operate), and **Alternatives considered** (each option with one or two lines on why it lost). Missing sections are a merge blocker. Each record carries a Status line (`Proposed`, `Accepted`, `Superseded by NNN`, `Deprecated`) and a Date line in ISO-8601. The target length is 60–120 lines; hard bounds are 40 and 150. ADRs are **immutable once accepted**. They are a historical record of what we chose and why at the time. If a later decision reverses an earlier one, write a new ADR — do not rewrite the old one. In the superseded record, change only the Status line to `Superseded by NNN` and add a one-line pointer to the new record; the Context, Decision, Consequences, and Alternatives stay as they were on the day the decision was made, because rewriting them erases the history the ADR exists to preserve. Typo fixes, broken-link repairs, and adding cross-references to later ADRs are fine; anything that changes the meaning is not. When an ADR references code or docs in another gyrum repo, link by GitHub URL, not by bare filename — the file tree of the other repo is not visible from the reader's position, and a bare filename is an invitation to a stale link. When a decision in one repo is implemented in another (the most common case for library-shaped decisions), the ADR lives where the decision was made and the stakeholders are; a pointer from the implementing repo's README back to the ADR URL closes the loop. Enforcement is advisory for now. `gyrum-review-pr` will warn — not block — on architecturally-shaped PRs that land without an ADR; the warning is the placeholder for a linter that lands in a future devtools PR. Until then, the rule is a review-time convention, and the three-persona review expects it to be applied. ## Mermaid diagrams — shape guidance Mermaid is the project's default diagram notation (see §Code fences and mermaid for why), but *any* diagram that sprawls off the edge of a sidebar viewer hurts more than it helps. The reader's canvas is narrow — especially on mobile or in the GitHub preview pane — and a diagram that forces horizontal scrolling is a diagram the reader will skip. Prefer a roughly square aspect ratio, between 4:3 and 1:1, so the picture lands on the page as a picture rather than a ribbon. A set of rules of thumb falls out of that constraint: - **Prefer `flowchart TB`** (top-bottom) for short chains of up to about seven nodes. Vertical flows stack cleanly inside a narrow reading column. - **Switch to `LR`** (left-right) only for genuinely linear pipelines of three to five steps. Beyond five, `LR` overflows the sidebar and becomes scroll-bait. - **Break up the diagram when it gets big.** More than about seven nodes is a hint to introduce a `subgraph` cluster or to split into two diagrams linked by prose. A tall column of more than ten rows should split. A wide row of more than five siblings should rotate to `TB` or split. - **Colour-code with `classDef`.** A flat monochrome diagram reads as a wiring schematic; a diagram with a small, consistent palette reads as a *picture* that the reader can orient inside. Reuse this palette across docs so readers build up muscle memory for what each colour means: ```text classDef success fill:#d4edda,stroke:#28a745 classDef warning fill:#fff3cd,stroke:#ffc107 classDef error fill:#f8d7da,stroke:#dc3545 classDef neutral fill:#e2e3e5,stroke:#6c757d ``` - **Cap sequence diagrams at four participants.** More than four and the swim-lanes run off the side; split into a Phase 1 / Phase 2 pair of diagrams instead. - **Annotate every edge in a state diagram with the triggering event.** An unlabeled transition breaks the "what caused this transition" story the diagram exists to tell. - **Provide a text alternative for complex diagrams.** One paragraph of plain-English summary below the diagram lets a reader whose mermaid render failed — or who is skimming on a phone — still get the gist. > [!TIP] > When in doubt, start with `flowchart TB`, seven nodes max, and one `classDef` applied to the two or three nodes the reader should focus on first. You can iterate from there; you rarely regret the square-aspect starting point. The demonstration diagram at the top of this document is a worked example of the guidance in this section: `flowchart TB`, two `subgraph` clusters, fewer than ten nodes total, and `classDef` used to distinguish "machine-checked" from "stylistic" from "outcome" nodes. ## Callouts and info blocks Prose is a linear medium, and some of the most important things a document has to say — a footgun, a pointer to a case study, a shortcut the reader will thank you for — want to break out of the line. GitHub-flavoured alert syntax is the project's default for these, because every viewer renders it natively and GitHub itself renders it inline on PR previews and file views: ```markdown > [!NOTE] > Side information that helps understanding but isn't critical. > [!TIP] > A shortcut, pattern, or convention that makes life easier. > [!IMPORTANT] > The reader needs to know this before doing anything else. > [!WARNING] > Potential footgun — easy to get wrong, consequences non-trivial. > [!CAUTION] > Destructive if done wrong. Stop and think before proceeding. ``` Beyond the five native alerts, a small set of gyrum-specific callouts using a nested blockquote plus a bold emoji-prefixed label covers the patterns that turn up repeatedly in our docs. The emoji come from the canonical icon vocabulary in §Icons in docs — do not invent new ones per document: ```markdown > **📖 Case study —** A PR, incident, or design that illustrates the point. > Pin these to real things that happened; they age well precisely because > they are factual. > **🧪 Example —** A worked example, usually code plus its output. > **🎯 Try this —** An action the reader can take right now to experience > what the doc describes. > **🕳️ Deep dive —** Optional tangent for readers who want more. Signal > that the reader can skip without losing the thread. > **⚠️ Pitfall —** A specific mistake repeatedly made in this area. Name > the mistake, name the fix. > **🔖 Glossary —** Inline term definition. Use when a technical term > appears for the first time and is not already in the global glossary. ``` The two notations compose: a `[!NOTE]` for "here's a fact the reader should be aware of" and a `**📖 Case study —**` for "here's a PR that grounds the fact in history" sit next to each other without fighting, because they answer different questions. > **📖 Case study —** An audit of project docs on 2026-04-24 found thirty-three distinct empty-state strings across the `docs/` tree — "nothing yet", "TBD", "coming soon", "—", and so on — with no consistent grammar, which is what prompted ADR-081's empty-state grammar. The lesson is that prose conventions drift by default, and a standards document that names the convention and gives the reader a copy-pasteable shape is the cheapest intervention that makes the drift stop. > [!WARNING] > Do not stack more than two callouts in a row. A page that is three-quarters callouts is a page whose author could not decide what was important; the reader ends up treating all of them as noise. ## Case studies and worked examples The two shapes — case study and worked example — do different jobs and should not be confused: - A **case study** is "this really happened and you can learn from it." Every case study cites a concrete PR or incident URL and closes on a one-sentence takeaway. Case studies age like fine wine because they are anchored to history — the PR number does not drift, the incident did not unhappen, and a reader six months from now can trace the reasoning back to the code that caused it. - A **worked example** is "here's what this looks like." Usually code plus its expected output. Tag the output fence as `text` so the reader can tell at a glance that it is output and not input; if the example is a command, show the command in `bash` and the output in `text`. Doc authors should aim for at least one case study *or* worked example per major concept. This is a rule of thumb, not a hard gate — some concepts are genuinely self-evident and need no illustration — but the rule of thumb is a useful default because the moment a reader sees a concept grounded in a real PR or a runnable snippet, their brain switches from "abstract text" to "thing I can reason about". The point of the ratio is not to hit a number; it is to keep the doc from becoming an unrelieved slab of prose. **🧪 Example —** The §Links rule says internal links must be relative paths to registered files. A compliant link and two non-compliant variants, side by side: ```text Good: [the gate stack](./gate-stack.md) Bad: [the gate stack](/docs/shared/gate-stack.md) # absolute — escapes viewer root Bad: [the gate stack](gate-stack.md) # bare — no ./ prefix ``` ## TL;DR block at document start Living documents longer than about two hundred lines should open — after the frontmatter, the H1, and the living-document header — with a short `## TL;DR` section that captures the decision or shape of the document in two to three sentences. The reader who has ten seconds before their meeting starts should come away with the headline even if they never scroll past the first screen. This is a preference, not a gate: the validator does not check for it. Short documents, reference tables, and ADRs (which have their own structural shape) do not need it. For everything else, a TL;DR is the single cheapest intervention that improves a doc's usefulness — the author has to decide what the point *actually* is, and the reader gets the answer without paying the cost of reading the whole file. The TL;DR at the top of this document is itself an example. ## Quick-reference tables Dense reference material — API shapes, status enum values, path conventions, command tables — belongs in a markdown table, not in prose. If the reader's primary intent is "remind me what the shape of X was", a table beats three paragraphs of explanation every time; the prose version is hostile to the reader's actual goal, which is to scan. The rule of thumb is this: if the content reads naturally as "X does Y, and Z does W, and Q does V", it is a table. Promote it. The icon vocabulary in §Icons in docs and the file list in `docs/shared/README.md` are both worked examples of this pattern — every reader of those sections arrives with a lookup intent, and a table is the shape that intent wants. A compact "which tool for which reader intent" reference: | Reader intent | Use | |---|---| | "What do I need to do?" | Imperative prose, ordered list | | "What does this *mean*?" | Explanatory prose | | "What was X's shape again?" | Quick-reference table | | "How does the flow go?" | Mermaid diagram (square aspect) | | "What really happened that time?" | Case-study callout | | "Can I skip this bit?" | Deep-dive callout | ## "See also" footer Every doc that names a cousin concept — another ADR, another playbook, another shared snippet, another primitive — should close with a short `## See also` section listing three to five cross-references. Not a dump of every link mentioned in the document; the three-to-five the reader is most likely to want to read *next*. The constraint is deliberate. A curated footer of the most useful next-reads is a feature; an exhaustive dump of every hyperlink in the doc is noise. If you cannot narrow your "See also" to five items, the doc is probably covering too much and should be split. ## Non-goals This document does not regulate prose voice, word count, or the tone of any given doc — consuming projects and their authors are free to choose what works for them. It does not prescribe a fixed outline for living documents, because different kinds of living documents need different shapes. It does not cap the number of documents in `docs/`, cap file size, or ban duplication between a doc and its source code. The structural rules at the top of this file are enforced mechanically; the stylistic guidance in the middle is preference; everything above that line is left to the author's judgment. ## See also - [`docs/shared/README.md`](./README.md) — why `docs/shared/` exists and how content reaches consuming projects. - [`docs/shared/gate-stack.md`](./gate-stack.md) — the structural validator that enforces the rules in the first half of this document. - [`docs/shared/workflow-boilerplate.md`](./workflow-boilerplate.md) — the developer loop inside which doc PRs get opened, reviewed, and merged. - [`docs/shared/check-stack.md`](./check-stack.md) — the full four-layer check stack, of which the doc-standards validator is one layer.

# Fleet standards — the version-badge contract Every Gyrum product is observable at a glance: which version is live, built when, and from which commit. Deploys are the single most common source of "why is this broken right now?", and the answer to that question almost always starts with "what actually shipped?" The version-badge contract is the fleet-wide answer: every product, regardless of stack, exposes the same structured build-identity on the same three surfaces, so an operator can triage any Gyrum service with the same three tools (curl, the browser footer, and the fleet widget) without relearning the conventions of each project. This document is the contract every product follows. It is written to be enforceable: a PR that claims to implement the contract but skips one of the three clauses below is incomplete. ## The contract The contract has three clauses. All three are non-negotiable for any product that ships a runtime — library-only repos and pure-CLI tools are exempt, because they have no deployment to verify. Products that ship both a backend and a UI implement all three; backend-only products implement clauses (a) alone; any product with an HTML surface implements (b) and (c) on top of that. ### a. `GET /api/version` endpoint Every product exposes an unauthenticated HTTP handler at `/api/version` returning JSON with exactly these five keys: ```json { "sha": "abc1234", "sha_full": "abc1234def5678901234567890abcdef12345678", "branch": "main", "built_at": "2026-04-23T18:42:00Z", "version_tag": "v0.33.0" } ``` Field shapes: - `sha` — 7-char short SHA, matches what GitHub shows in commit lists. - `sha_full` — 40-char full SHA, suitable for building a commit URL. - `branch` — branch name the binary/bundle was built from (usually `main` in production). - `built_at` — ISO8601 UTC timestamp of the build, e.g. `2026-04-23T18:42:00Z`. - `version_tag` — `git describe --tags --always` output; produces a human-friendly marker like `v0.33.0` on tagged releases and a short SHA on untagged commits. The endpoint is public by design. The same values are already embedded in the rendered HTML (clause c) and in startup logs, so the endpoint adds no new information disclosure — and requiring authentication to answer "what version is live?" is the wrong trade-off against the value of "anyone on the team can `curl /api/version` from their laptop in an incident". When git was unavailable at build time (shallow CI clones, distroless containers, `go build ./...` without the Makefile), each field falls back to the literal string `"unknown"`. The endpoint still returns HTTP 200 and the same JSON shape — staleness is obvious rather than silent, and downstream tooling never has to distinguish "the endpoint is missing" from "the endpoint is there but the build was stale". ### b. Footer visible in any UI Products with a UI surface render a small, muted footer at the bottom of the application shell showing ` · `. The entire footer is a clickable link to `https://github.com/gyrum-labs//commit/`. Use existing design tokens for colour and spacing — `--text-muted` for the foreground, `--font-mono` for the typeface, the mode-tokens border colour for the top edge. No animation, no emoji, no background fill: the footer is calm reference furniture, not a notification. The footer always renders, even when the injected values are `"unknown"`; the link target is still valid (it will 404 on GitHub, which is the correct signal that this build is not reproducible from a commit). A `data-testid="version-footer"` attribute is required so e2e tests can select it without relying on CSS class names that might churn. ### c. `` in HTML head Products serving HTML must include two meta tags in the document head: ```html ``` The tags are the machine-readable hook for monitoring and fleet-wide scans. `curl -s https:/// | grep gyrum-sha` is the canonical one-liner for "what SHA is this instance serving?" — it works without parsing JSON, without application auth, and without knowing the product's specific URL conventions. Every page the product serves must carry both tags; a tag that only appears on the landing page is a bug, because the grep will fail for anyone deep-linking into the app. ## Stack-specific implementation The mechanism is whatever the framework provides. The shape — five JSON keys, the footer, the two meta tags — is identical across stacks so that a single fleet widget (see "Why this matters") can aggregate every product's build-identity without per-product adapters. ### SvelteKit + Vite Reference implementation: [ai-frontend PR #141](https://github.com/gyrum-labs/ai-frontend/pull/141). Four files carry the entire contract. `vite.config.ts` captures git values at build time and feeds them through Vite's `define` block as `VITE_*` build-time constants: ```ts import { execSync } from 'node:child_process'; function git(cmd: string, fallback = 'unknown'): string { try { return execSync(`git ${cmd}`, { stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'ignore'] }) .toString() .trim(); } catch { return fallback; } } const GIT_SHA_FULL = git('rev-parse HEAD'); const GIT_SHA_SHORT = git('rev-parse --short HEAD'); const GIT_BRANCH = git('rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD'); const VERSION_TAG = git('describe --tags --always'); const BUILD_TIME = new Date().toISOString(); export default defineConfig({ plugins: [sveltekit(), svelteTesting()], define: { 'import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_SHA_FULL': JSON.stringify(GIT_SHA_FULL), 'import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_SHA_SHORT': JSON.stringify(GIT_SHA_SHORT), 'import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_BRANCH': JSON.stringify(GIT_BRANCH), 'import.meta.env.VITE_BUILD_TIME': JSON.stringify(BUILD_TIME), 'import.meta.env.VITE_VERSION_TAG': JSON.stringify(VERSION_TAG) } }); ``` `src/lib/version.ts` re-exports the constants and a `versionSummary()` helper: ```ts export const GIT_SHA_FULL: string = import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_SHA_FULL || 'unknown'; export const GIT_SHA_SHORT: string = import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_SHA_SHORT || 'unknown'; export const GIT_BRANCH: string = import.meta.env.VITE_GIT_BRANCH || 'unknown'; export const BUILD_TIME: string = import.meta.env.VITE_BUILD_TIME || 'unknown'; export const VERSION_TAG: string = import.meta.env.VITE_VERSION_TAG || 'unknown'; export function versionSummary(): string { return `${GIT_SHA_SHORT} · ${formatBuildTime()}`; } ``` `src/routes/+layout.svelte` renders the two meta tags and the footer: ```svelte
{versionSummary()}
``` `src/routes/api/version/+server.ts` serves the JSON endpoint: ```ts import { json } from '@sveltejs/kit'; import type { RequestHandler } from './$types'; import { GIT_SHA_FULL, GIT_SHA_SHORT, GIT_BRANCH, BUILD_TIME, VERSION_TAG } from '$lib/version.js'; export const GET: RequestHandler = () => { return json({ sha: GIT_SHA_SHORT, sha_full: GIT_SHA_FULL, branch: GIT_BRANCH, built_at: BUILD_TIME, version_tag: VERSION_TAG }); }; ``` ### Go Reference implementation: [ai-research PR #592](https://github.com/gyrum-labs/ai-research/pull/592). The pattern is `-ldflags -X` injection into an `internal/version` package, plus a handler registered on the service mux. This document is the written contract for the **metadata-aware capture**: what the producer writes beside a capture, what the consumer requires before it trusts it, what "unavailable" means, and how a metadata-aware capture is told apart from a legacy one. Owner: the metadata-aware capture contract installed by `lib/persona-review-test-evidence.sh` (`_persona_capture_install_contract`) on the native Shell capture entry point (`mutation_run_suite`), and its consumer in the same file (`_persona_test_evidence_render_from_sink`). The producer's own library (`lib/mutation-score-lib.sh`) is held by an open devtools PR, so the contract is installed where the capture sink is consumed rather than inside the producer; the recorded facts are still the producer's own published facts, read at capture time from the invocation that produced the capture. ## Why the contract exists The producer knows four facts about a run that the reviewer needs: the time allowance that **actually applied** to that invocation, where that allowance came from, the **original exit code**, and the **failure class the producer observed**. A capture that carries only the log and the exit code cannot be told apart from an assertion failure, and cannot be told apart from a failure at a *different* registered budget. The reviewer then reads a timeout at one bound as a breach of another bound — the dark-factory PR #2643 incident. The contract therefore carries exactly those four facts, plus the **provenance** that binds them to the capture they belong to. ## The sidecar A metadata-aware capture is a triple in the capture sink: ``` <sink>/<slug>.log the captured output bytes (unchanged, unchanged shape) <sink>/<slug>.rc the original exit code the producer observed <sink>/<slug>.meta the metadata-aware sidecar (this contract) ``` `<slug>` is the capture file path with `/` replaced by `_` (the same transform `mutation_run_suite` and the consumer already use for `.log`/`.rc`). ### Sidecar fields The sidecar is a `key=value` line format, one field per line. The first `=` separates the key from its value; later `=` characters remain part of that value. **All seven fields are required**; a sidecar missing any of them, or carrying an empty value for one of them, is malformed and renders as unavailable. | Field | Required | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `schema` | yes | `persona-capture-provenance-v1`. The consumer accepts this exact value; any other value is malformed. | | `allowance_seconds` | yes | The invocation allowance that **actually applied** to this execution, in whole seconds (≥ 1). It is *not* a registered budget the suite might be subject to elsewhere. | | `allowance_source` | yes | Where that allowance came from — the setting or caller that supplied it (e.g. `MUTATION_SCORE_BASELINE_TIMEOUT`, `persona-test-evidence`). It is **not** a model or provider identifier. | | `original_exit` | yes | The exit code the producer observed for the invocation, before any interpretation (0–255). | | `producer_class` | yes | The producer-observed failure class, verbatim. One of `passed`, `test-failed`, `setup-failed`, `invocation-failed`, `timeout`, `signal-or-infrastructure`. | | `command` | yes | The command the producer ran for this invocation (already redacted and bounded by the producer). | | `log_sha256` | yes | The SHA-256 of the captured `.log` bytes. This is the **provenance binding**: it ties the four facts to this exact capture. | ### The producer's published fields The contract reads the producer's own published result fields, taken from `lib/mutation-score-lib.sh` (`mutation_run_suite`): | Field | Published as | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `MUTATION_RUN_EXIT_CLASS` | one of `passed`, `test-failed`, `setup-failed`, `invocation-failed`, `timeout`, `signal-or-infrastructure` | the failure class the producer observed for the invocation it just ran | | `MUTATION_RUN_COMMAND` | the command it ran, redacted and bounded by the producer before publication | which invocation the facts describe | | `MUTATION_RUN_DIAGNOSTIC` | one bounded line with `command=`, `timeout=`, `timeout_source=`, `exit=` and `class=` | the producer's own per-invocation record | The regression test pins the producer's published class vocabulary against the accepted set above, so a producer-side vocabulary change is caught at this boundary instead of silently demoting a capture to "unavailable". ### Invocation granularity A capture that holds several files runs the producer once per file, so each capture carries the facts of its own invocation. Every suite file still executes exactly once, and the capture order and the stop-at-the-first-failure behaviour are the producer's own; what changes is the runner's batching, not the suite's execution count. ### Where the sidecar is written The sidecar is written at capture time, by the same function that runs the producer invocation: the facts are read from the producer's published result fields for that invocation, never reconstructed afterwards. The contract covers the captures taken after this module is sourced; a caller that runs the producer before it is loaded keeps the legacy log/rc-only protocol. A capture can therefore never carry another invocation's facts, and a producer that returns before publishing a class records an empty class — which renders as unavailable, never as a fabricated class. ### Provenance Provenance is the evidence that `allowance_seconds`, `allowance_source`, `original_exit` and `producer_class` belong to **the same invocation** as the accompanying `.log` and `.rc`. It is established by two checks the consumer performs on every metadata-aware capture: 1. `log_sha256` equals the SHA-256 of the `.log` file that is rendered beside it. 2. `original_exit` equals the content of the `.rc` file that is rendered beside it. A sidecar that parses correctly but was produced by a **different invocation** fails check 1 and renders as unavailable. Nothing about the other invocation's allowance, source or class is attributed to this one. ## The consumer's rules * **Metadata-aware capture** (a `.meta` sidecar is present and valid): the rendered entry shows the outcome word, the invocation allowance that applied, the allowance source, the original exit code and the producer's class verbatim. The class is never renamed, aliased, merged or re-derived from the exit code; the consumer infers no assertion cause from an arbitrary nonzero exit. * **Timeout** reads as **INCOMPLETE** at the allowance that actually applied. It never reads as an assertion failure and never as a failure at another registered budget. * **Unavailable**: a `.meta` sidecar that is missing a required field, malformed (a non-numeric allowance, an unknown class, a wrong schema, an unknown key), or mismatched (its digest or exit does not belong to the rendered log/rc) renders as a visible statement that the provenance could not be trusted. It never supplies success, never supplies a budget figure, and never silently falls back to looking like verified legacy evidence. * **Legacy capture** (no `.meta` sidecar — an established non-Shell caller, or a stored legacy corpus): rendered exactly as before, byte for byte. The consumer asserts no allowance, source, class or provenance for it and adds no "unavailable" wording. ## Metadata-aware vs legacy — how they are told apart A filesystem entry at the `.meta` path expresses metadata intent. A regular sidecar must still pass the field, digest and exit checks; an empty or partial regular file, a directory or a dangling symlink renders as unavailable. A nonregular entry is rejected without reading it. Truncating a regular file leaves its metadata intent present; truncation does not unlink it. Producer execution count, order, original return and stop behavior remain unchanged when a metadata write fails. There is no flag, environment variable or caller opt-in. A completely absent sidecar still selects the established legacy protocol. This discriminator cannot infer metadata intent when no entry exists; it does not claim to recover an entirely missing marker or an unwritable-parent history from log/rc alone. A legacy capture is any capture that did not select this contract — a log/rc-only capture from an established non-Shell caller, or a stored legacy corpus. Its rendered bytes are unchanged, so a legacy corpus captured before this contract existed still renders identically. ## Privacy The rendered evidence carries the four invocation facts and the bounded case lines / five-line tail the renderer already displayed. It never carries the full private raw log, and never carries environment, provider or credential data. The sidecar's `command` field is the producer's own published command (`MUTATION_RUN_COMMAND`), which the producer redacts and bounds before it publishes it. The stored log/rc sink adapter retains the fixed legacy rendering. Standalone internal diagnostics keep the current outcome-before-case rendering; a metadata-aware sink emits its producer-observed outcome once, without a second exit-code inference. Focused selection still delegates through that sink adapter.

Run scripts/update-docs.sh to refresh. --> # The three-command workflow Every gyrum project uses the same short developer loop: start work, run the review, complete the PR. There are three commands — `gyrum-start-work`, `gyrum-review-pr`, and `gyrum-complete-pr` — and together they cover the full journey from "I want to change something" to "the change is on main with a new version tag". The shape is deliberate. Each command is a checkpoint with a defined side effect: a branch exists, a review has run, a version has been bumped. And because the loop is identical across every gyrum repository, a developer who has used it once can drop into any other gyrum project without re-learning how changes get shipped. ## Start work ```bash gyrum-start-work add-user-auth ``` `gyrum-start-work <feature-name>` creates a new branch named `feat/<feature-name>` from an up-to-date local `main`, pushes it to the remote, and immediately opens a draft pull request against `main`. This all happens before you have written a single line of code. That timing is intentional. The PR becomes the living description of the work from the moment the idea is committed to: it is visible to anyone watching the repository, it is where the review personas eventually land their verdicts, and it removes the small-but-annoying decision of "when is this ready to open a PR?" — the answer is "right now, at the start, as a draft". The draft state tells the review panel and other humans that the work is in progress, and a later command will flip it to ready once the review has passed. ## Work What happens between "start work" and "review" is ordinary coding, with one quiet backstop: the `pre-push` hook that `gyrum-setup` installs runs on every push and refuses to let you push a broken branch. The exact checks depend on the project stack, but the core is always the same — if the build fails or the tests fail, the push is blocked and you see the failure immediately, before anyone else has reason to look at the branch. This is not meant to be annoying. It is a protective layer: the hook catches regressions at the cheapest possible moment, on your own machine, where the fix loop is fast and nobody else is waiting. The hook is deliberately light — build and test only — so it stays fast on every push; the heavier suite (linters, coverage, secret scans, complexity, security) is reserved for `gyrum-review-pr`, which runs it once, at the moment it matters, on top of the full AI review panel. There is a second way to work on a change, which is the AI-assisted path via `gyrum-implement "<task>"`. Running this starts a guided loop: Claude asks you a handful of clarifying questions about what the feature needs, you answer in plain text, and the script synthesises a structured specification — requirements, acceptance criteria, open questions — and writes it straight to the PR description *before* any code is written. Only after you confirm the spec does implementation start, and it starts test-first. The important idea is that the PR exists as a requirements document first, a code change second. That order lets the author and the reviewers read and refine the spec on GitHub, in context, before any commits arrive to argue with. ## Review ```bash gyrum-review-pr ``` `gyrum-review-pr` is the moment a change is put up against the gate. Running it is not optional — it is the script that drives every layer of the gate, including the calls that post formal GitHub reviews on the author's behalf, so merge to `main` is blocked until it has been run and passed on the latest commit. Running `gyrum-review-pr` first runs the structural checks, because there is no point asking an AI reviewer to read a diff that does not compile, and exits with a clear failure message if any blocking check fails. Once the structural layer is green, the four review personas run in parallel. Each one reads the diff with its own narrow mandate — Priya for security, Marcus for architecture, Lin for test and doc quality, Dana for reader onboarding — and each one files a verdict. Priya, Marcus, and Lin post their verdicts as real GitHub reviews, using persona-specific personal access tokens, and those reviews are what branch protection actually counts. Dana posts her feedback as a PR comment, clearly labelled as advisory, and her verdict gates the local script's exit code but not GitHub's formal approval threshold. The reasoning behind the split is explained in `gate-stack.md`. The structural layer is a suite of mechanical checks; the exact set depends on the project stack, but every consumer runs these blocking categories: - **Build + test** — the project compiles and its tests pass on the PR's head commit. - **Lint + static analysis** — `staticcheck`/`eslint` and the language-specific vetters catch style and common-bug patterns. - **Coverage** — diff coverage on changed statements must clear the floor from `lib/thresholds.conf`. - **Size + shape** — new files under the file-line cap, new functions under the cyclomatic cap, the whole PR under the line/file caps. - **Secret + binary scan** — no credentials in the diff, no multi-megabyte blobs outside LFS. <!-- the /tmp path is a runtime-artifact location, not a repo-relative path; it intentionally does not resolve in the consumer tree --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> - **Viewer-validator** — every markdown file under `docs/` must satisfy the mechanical contract in `doc-standards.md` (index registration, frontmatter on living docs, single H1 with no skipped heading levels, tagged code fences, relative internal links to registered files, and seeded templates filled in). Run by `viewer-validator.py` and blocking; a JSON report lands at `/tmp/gyrum-viewer-validator.json` for diagnostics. Verdicts from the AI panel appear inline as the script runs, so you can see each persona's call the moment it comes in. If one of them requests changes, the script exits with a non-zero code and prints what to fix. The right response is not to rewrite history or amend the PR — it is to make a new commit that addresses the feedback, push it, and run `gyrum-review-pr` again. The script uses incremental review, which means each persona only re-reads the diff between its last verdict and the new HEAD; a small fix does not force the whole PR to be re-reviewed from scratch. When the threshold is met — the structural gate green **and** at least two of the three formal approvals (Priya/Marcus/Lin) **and** Dana's advisory pass — the script updates the PR body from the commit log, flips the PR out of draft state, and prints a success message telling you to run the completion command. Merge to `main` is blocked until all three of those conditions hold. ## Complete ```bash gyrum-complete-pr ``` `gyrum-complete-pr` is the final checkpoint. It waits until the required approvals are in place on GitHub, performs the merge, syncs your local `main`, derives the next patch version from the `VERSION` file's MAJOR.MINOR anchor plus the count of merges since the anchor was last changed, tags the merge commit, and pushes the tag. The tag is not a cosmetic touch; it is how every merged change gets a unique, visible version identifier, which in turn is what makes rollback and audit tractable without any additional ceremony. If something breaks on `main` next week, "when did this start?" has a precise answer, because every merge since has a tag attached to it. Because the patch number is *derived* at tag time instead of written back to the file, two `gyrum-complete-pr` runs for different PRs merging in parallel cannot collide — each tags its own merge commit with its own deterministic count. ## Thresholds <!-- consumer may not have .gyrum/debt-thresholds.json yet — overridable per-project, optional --> <!-- doc-truth: ignore-next --> The numeric thresholds that govern the gate — coverage minimums, diff-size limits, file-length caps, cyclomatic complexity, function length, directory file count — live in a single file: `lib/thresholds.conf` inside the devtools checkout. Review-pr.sh sources it directly, and the CLAUDE.md template that `gyrum-setup` drops into a new project is rendered from the same values. That means the number in your CLAUDE.md and the number the gate will enforce cannot drift — they come from the same place. A project can override any individual threshold by writing `.gyrum/debt-thresholds.json` in its own tree, and the override layers on top of the SSOT at review time. The specific values are intentionally not listed here: if you want to know what they are right now, read `lib/thresholds.conf`. ## Escape hatches, and the ones that do not exist Real life occasionally asks for exceptions, and it is worth being clear about which ones the workflow supports and which it does not. The answer is short: there is deliberately no developer-time flag to bypass the AI review panel. If you want to know whether the structural layer is happy, push and let the `pre-push` hook run its checks locally; that is the designed-in shortcut. If you want to know what the panel will say, run `gyrum-review-pr` — including while iterating — and let each re-run use the incremental review to keep the feedback loop tight. Shortcuts that skip the hooks entirely — `git push --no-verify` is the obvious one — are not forbidden, because sometimes an emergency is real. They are, however, not invisible. A push that skipped the gate should leave a note in the PR description explaining why and a follow-up debt entry via `gyrum-file-debt` so the shortcut is accounted for. The point is not that the hooks are sacred. The point is that the gate is the mechanism by which everyone downstream trusts the merge, and skipping it silently breaks that trust for every reader of the log who comes after you. Leave a trail and the shortcut costs nothing; hide it and the shortcut costs the team's confidence in the rest of the history. ## In one sentence The three commands are the ergonomic front end of the system described in `gate-stack.md`: the start command puts a draft PR on the board, the review command runs the gate, the completion command ships the change with a new version, and branch protection on the server is what makes sure the steps actually happened.

This guide is for someone who has never run this project before. It takes about ten minutes to read and leaves you able to play the adventure yourself and understand what the experiment is measuring. ## Concepts Five nouns to hold in your head. `SPEC.md` Part 0 is the long version; this is the short one. **Adventure.** The complete definition of one game — its rooms, objects, doors, actions and goals. It is *pure data*: no logic, no code, just declarations the engine reads. *Not* a running program, and *not* the thing under test. **Kernel.** The pure engine: it takes the current state and one command and returns the next state. It never guesses, never asks the model anything, and never changes its mind. *Not* a game framework — it is small enough to read in one sitting. **State.** Everything true right now: which room the agent is in, what it carries, which doors are open. A plain value that can be printed and compared. *Not* a process. **Observation.** The part of the state the agent is allowed to see. Deliberately *smaller* than the state — the agent cannot see inside a closed locker. *Not* the state, and not a summary of it. **Turn.** One action and its consequences. The kernel's only unit of time. *Not* a "round" of anything. ## Getting started **Prerequisites.** Node 20 or newer. Git. That is all the project itself needs; an LLM provider key is only needed for the agent runs, and the mock provider needs none. ```sh git clone https://github.com/gyrum-labs/research-text-adventure-ai.git cd research-text-adventure-ai npm install ``` **First launch.** Play the adventure yourself: ```sh npm run play ``` You should see this: ``` Briefing Room A windowless office. A desk, a wall notice, and a door south to the service corridor. You can see: keycard, bulletin, desk Exits: south → Service Corridor Carrying: (nothing) Objectives: - Disarm the bomb [not done] - Recover the case [not done] > _ ``` **Confirming it is healthy.** The suite is the check. It must be green before anything else is trusted: ```sh npm run check # typecheck + lint + tests ``` ## First use The simplest end-to-end workflow: play the adventure, then watch a model attempt the same thing. **Step 1 — play it.** Type commands at the `>` prompt. The ten commands that finish the mission: ``` take keycard · go corridor · open locker · take cutters · read manual unlock vault door with keycard · go vault · cut yellow wire with cutters unlock safe with 4821 · take case ``` **Step 2 — watch a model try.** The same adventure, the same engine, no extra help: ```sh npm run agent -- --provider mock # offline, free, deterministic npm run agent -- --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4.5 ``` **Step 3 — read the evidence.** Every run writes a transcript and a metrics file under `runs/`. The transcript is the record you can check: ``` {"type":"header","scenario":"mission-impossible","provider":"anthropic","seed":7,…} {"type":"command","turn":1,"raw":"take keycard","verb":"take","args":{"target":"keycard"}} {"type":"events","turn":1,"data":[{"type":"action_succeeded","message":"You pocket the keycard."}]} {"type":"state","turn":1,"hash":"sha256:…"} ``` And you can check it yourself — replaying a transcript re-runs its commands through the engine and compares the hash chain: ```sh npm run replay -- runs/<file>.jsonl ``` ## Common workflows | Flow | Command | What you get | |---|---|---| | Play the adventure | `npm run play` | The game at the terminal | | Watch a model attempt it | `npm run agent -- --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4.5` | A transcript and metrics under `runs/` | | Run with no network or cost | `npm run agent -- --provider mock` | The same pipeline, deterministic | | Check a recorded run | `npm run replay -- runs/<file>.jsonl` | Exit 0 if the engine reproduced the run exactly | | Sweep the experiment matrix | `npm run sweep` | `results/summary.json` and `results/summary.md` | | Read the docs in a browser | `pydocs .` | This repository's Markdown, with search and Mermaid | For the full walkthrough of the experiment series, start at [`experiments/README.md`](../experiments/README.md) — each experiment has its own README with the idea, the tests and the acceptance criteria. ## Troubleshooting **`npm run play` says the command is not found.** The project is not installed yet. Run `npm install` in the repository root. **The agent's first command is nonsense.** Expected, and informative. That is why `invalidActionRate` is a metric: the agent is told what it did wrong and gets another turn. If the run ends immediately, look for a `parse_error` event in the transcript. **`npm run agent` fails with an authentication error.** The provider key is missing from the environment. Use `--provider mock` to exercise the whole pipeline without a key, and check the key's environment variable name against the provider adapter's documentation. **The replay says the hash chain does not match.** Something changed between the run and the replay — most often the adventure data itself, which is hashed into the transcript header. If the adventure was edited, the old transcript legitimately no longer replays. The transcript header records the adventure hash so this is detectable rather than mysterious. **A run ends with `budget_exhausted` and no clear failure.** The agent used its turns without winning. The failure classifier will tell you which category it fell into; look for `F5` (exploration failure) or `F7` (budget exhaustion). **The docs viewer shows an old version of a document.** Readers cache the index at startup. Restart the reader after adding or removing documents.
